papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: AbstractFor nearly 50 years, scientists have sought to exploit messenger RNA (mRNA) as a therapeutic tool, overcoming major challenges related to instability, delivery, and inflammatory reactions. A major breakthrough came with the incorporation of modified nucleosides, particularly pseudouridine, during in vitro mRNA synthesis, which markedly improved stability, translation efficiency, and tolerability. The clinical success of mRNA technology was demonstrated in 2020 with the development of highly effective and safe COVID-19 vaccines, administered to over a billion individuals worldwide. These achievements inaugurated a new era in molecular medicine. In this review, we revisit the historical development of mRNA delivery into human cells and discuss the emergence of mRNA as a gene-therapy approach. In fact, beyond vaccination, mRNA platforms are rapidly expanding toward protein replacement therapies for genetic disorders and innovative strategies for cancer treatment. We summarize advances in synthetic mRNA design and optimization, delivery vehicles, and administration strategies that enable therapeutic applications. Finally, we highlight current limitations, technological challenges, and future opportunities, emphasizing how mRNA-based technologies have become powerful tools for studying gene function and developing next-generation precision therapies. IntroductionSince the discovery of the RNA functions as information messenger, scientists have worked extensively to understand how mRNA could be used to treat human diseases. These efforts faced many challenges until 2008, when Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman made the fundamental discovery indicating that the incorporation of modified nucleosides into the mRNA molecules (particularly N1-methylpseudouridine and 5-methylcytidine) could overcome exacerbated inflammatory reactions and, together with the development of lipid nanoparticles as a delivery system, rendered these molecules therapeutically viable (Karikó et al., 2005, 2008). In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the approval of the first mRNA-based vaccines for human use represented a major milestone, highlighting the therapeutic potential of mRNA technology. The vaccination of more than one billion individuals worldwide demonstrated not only high efficacy in protecting humans against specific viral pathogens but also demonstrated the safety and feasibility of using mRNA molecules for broader biomedical applications, including therapies for human genetic and acquired diseases. mRNA-based therapeutics offer several advantages, including the absence of genomic integration, high versatility, and rapid development and production. However, as with any other therapeutic strategy, important challenges remain, particularly regarding cell- and tissue-specific delivery and precise modulation of the immune system (Wei et al., 2023). This review focuses on recent advances in the use of mRNA molecules as potential gene therapy tools, highlights current strategies and future perspectives. The application of mRNA molecules as vaccines against cancer is also summarized. In contrast, mRNA vaccines for infectious diseases are addressed primarily from a historical perspective, emphasizing key discoveries related to the delivery of these molecules to cells and organisms. Readers interested in recent developments in vaccines for infectious diseases or cancer are encouraged to consult comprehensive and up-to-date reviews on the topic (Ali, 2025; Quan et al., 2025). The history of mRNA delivery systemsThe messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) was first described in 1961 by François Gros and colleagues (Gros et al., 1961). Seventeen years later, in 1978, mRNA was successfully transfected into cells, when mRNA encoding a globin-like protein was delivered into human epithelial carcinoma (HEp-2) cells using liposomes, resulting in detectable protein translation (Ostro et al., 1978). Subsequently, in vitro synthesis of mRNA encoding Xenopus β-globin using SP6 bacteriophage RNA polymerase was achieved from complementary DNA (cDNA). Injection of these mRNA molecules into frog oocyte cytoplasm resulted in efficient protein translation. Importantly, this process was shown to depend on the presence of 5’cap modification, whereas deletion of most of the 3’ flanking region, including the poly(A) tail, did not completely abolish protein synthesis (Krieg and Melton, 1984). Further advances demonstrated that in vitro-transcribed (IVT) luciferase mRNA could be introduced into NIH 3T3 mouse cells using a lipid-based delivery system, leading to measurable luciferase activity (Malone et al., 1989). Shortly thereafter, direct injection of IVT mRNA (encoding chloramphenicol acetyltransferase, luciferase, and beta-galactosidase) into the skeletal muscle of mice also resulted in successful in vivo protein expression (Wolff et al., 1990). Despite these early breakthroughs, progress in mRNA-based therapeutics remained limited for many years due to significant technical challenges, including liability and strong endogenous inflammatory reactions (Sahin et al., 2014).Building upon these early advances, the pioneer experiments for mRNA therapy were reported in 1992 using Brattleboro rats, a strain that served as a model for diabetes insipidus, due to the inability to produce the hormone vasopressin. Direct intracerebral injection of vasopressin-encoding mRNA restored hormone production and effectively reversed disease symptoms within hours, with therapeutic effects lasting up to five days after treatment (Jirikowski et al., 1992). This study provided one of the earliest proofs of concept that exogenous mRNA could be used to transiently replace defective or absent proteins in vivo.Parallel efforts explored the potential of mRNA as a vaccination platform. In 1993, the IVT influenza virus nucleoprotein mRNA encapsulated into liposomes was shown to induce a robust immune response in mice, stimulating the production of cytotoxic T lymphocytes, essential for eliminating virus-infected cells (Martinon et al., 1993). These findings highlighted the capacity of mRNA to stimulate antigen-specific cellular immunity and suggested its potential application in infectious disease prevention.Shortly thereafter, the feasibility of mRNA-based cancer vaccines was demonstrated. A capped, polyadenylated, and stabilized mRNA encoding a tumor-associated carcinoembryonic antigen was delivered into mouse fibroblast cells via liposome-mediated transfection, resulting in efficient antigen expression. In pilot in vivo experiments, immunization with this mRNA triggered antigen-specific immune responses and protected mice from colon carcinoma cells engineered to express the same antigen (Conry et al., 1995). These results provided early evidence that mRNA vaccination could generate protective antitumor immunity.Together, these pioneering studies established the conceptual and experimental foundations for mRNA-based therapeutics and vaccination, although widespread application remained limited by technical challenges related to mRNA stability, delivery efficiency, and exacerbated inflammation.Concurrently, several post-transcriptional nucleoside modifications in RNA were identified, such as the deamination of adenosines and cytidines, which were shown to influence mRNA translation efficiency and regulation (Kiss, 2001). Numerous modified ribonucleotides were subsequently described for the major cellular RNA classes, including tRNAs, rRNAs, mRNA, and snRNAs, most of which are introduced post-transcriptionally (Limbach et al., 1994; Kiss, 2001). These modifications were demonstrated to play essential structural and functional roles. In tRNAs, for example, nucleotide modifications promote accurate anticodon-codon pairing and enhance both the efficiency and fidelity of translation (Agris, 1996; Kiss, 2001).In the early 2000s, fundamental discoveries in understanding mRNA inflammatory reactions emerged from studies of Karikó and Weissman. Their work demonstrated that IVT RNA molecules activate human Toll-like receptor (TLR) 3, thereby triggering innate immune responses (Karikó et al., 2004). Similarly, bacterial RNA was also shown to stimulate innate immunity and inflammation, while mRNA and tRNA derived from eukaryotic sources failed to activate cultured human dendritic cells (DC) (Koski et al., 2004). TLRs are key initiators of adaptive immune responses, promoting T-cell differentiation into T helper 1 effector cells against microbial infections through recognition of foreign nucleic acids (Medzhitov, 2001). Importantly, activation of these receptors by exogenous mRNA significantly limits protein expression due to cell death following cellular transfection, representing a major obstacle for therapeutic applications. Subsequent studies by Karikó and Weissman led to a seminal discovery demonstrating that the incorporation of modified nucleosides-including 5-methylcytidine (m5C), N6-methyladenosine (m6A), 5-methyluridine (m5U), 2-thiouridine (s2U), and pseudouridine-during in vitro mRNA synthesis markedly suppresses TLR-mediated inflammatory reactions (Karikó et al., 2005). Their work furthermore showed that mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA) stimulates monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MDDCs), whereas mammalian tRNA did not induce detectable levels of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α). This difference is likely explained by the structural similarity between mitochondrial and bacterial RNA, both of which contain relatively few nucleoside modifications and therefore act as potent DC activators. In contrast, tRNAs are highly modified and show little or no activity of DC activation (Karikó et al., 2005). Further advances demonstrated that mRNA containing pseudouridine exhibits significantly enhanced translational capacity compared to unmodified transcripts, when introduced in mammalian cells, cell-free lysates, or following intravenous administration into mice. Importantly, only unmodified mRNA induced strong immunogenic responses, including high levels of interferon alpha production (Karikó et al., 2008). In Figure 1, a historical timeline for these discoveries, which turned possible the use of mRNA for vaccine and therapy, is presented.Collectively, these findings established that incorporation of modified nucleosides, particularly pseudouridine, during in vitro mRNA synthesis was critical for reducing innate immune recognition, cell death and activation of deleterious inflammatory responses, which resulted in enhanced expression of proteins encoded by the exogenous mRNA and, thereby, enabling the development of effective therapeutic mRNA platforms. Figure 2 illustrates the biological outcomes of transfection with RNA molecules synthesized with pseudouridine, namely elimination of innate inflammatory responses, and improvement of translation efficiency. Figure 1 - The timeline history of mRNA gene therapy. Figure 2 - Representative scheme of the biological outcome of uridine substitution with pseudouridine. Replacement of uridine with pseudouridine during in vitro mRNA synthesis provides significant advantages when the mRNA is introduced into cells. These benefits include higher translational efficiency, leading to increased protein production, as well as a reduced inflammatory response. Figure adapted from the Nobel Prize announcement website. https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2023/advanced-information/. As a consequence of the landmark discoveries made by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, along with their broader outstanding contributions to the development of nucleoside-modified mRNA technology, they were awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2023/). Their work was fundamental by enabling the development of effective mRNA vaccines, including those used against COVID-19. The first-in-human clinical trial for an mRNA vaccine encoding the rabies virus glycoprotein (CV7201) was conducted before any signs of the COVID-19 pandemic and published in 2017 (Alberer et al., 2017). In this study, female and male volunteers with no prior history of rabies vaccination received escalating doses administered intradermally or intramuscularly using needle-syringe or needle-free devices, followed by a booster dose after one year. This trial represented the first demonstration of an effective mRNA-based vaccine tested in humans. The vaccine successfully induced antibody responses against the viral antigen and proved to be safe and well-tolerated (Alberer et al., 2017). Of note, in 2018, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based therapy carrying a small interfering RNA (siRNA) (patisiran, Onpattro®) (Akinc et al., 2019). This drug, indicated for the treatment of polyneuropathy associated with hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis in adults, inhibits the hepatic synthesis of transthyretin (mutant and wild-type). It acts by specifically binding to a genetically conserved sequence in the 3’ untranslated region of transthyretin messenger RNA (Hoy, 2018). This approval marked the first regulatory validation of an LNP system designed to deliver an RNA molecule in humans and demonstrated that such platforms could safely and effectively enable systemic nucleic acid delivery. Indeed, incorporation of the mRNA molecules into ionizable LNPs conferred both increased stability to the molecules and, simultaneously, offer a highly efficient approach to introduce mRNA molecules into the cytoplasm of transfected cells. These advances were critical for clinical translation and later supported the development and approval of mRNA-based vaccines for human use. In December 2020, the biotech companies Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna received emergency use authorization for the COVID-19 mRNA-based vaccines from the U.S. FDA and from the European Medicines Agency (EMA). In both vaccines, the nucleoside-modified mRNA encoding the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein is administered intramuscularly using lipid nanoparticle-formulation. These groundbreaking vaccines played a pivotal role in mitigating the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Their rapid development, high efficacy, and adaptability to emerging viral variants established a new paradigm for vaccine design and highlighted the potential of mRNA platforms for combating future infectious diseases and other medical conditions (Lamb, 2021). mRNA-based therapy for protein replacement Several human genetic disorders result from mutations leading to deficiencies in the activity or the production of specific enzymes. A transformative therapeutic strategy for many of these conditions has been enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), which involves the application of recombinant forms of the missing enzyme to patients, with important clinical benefits. However, ERT presents several limitations, including reactogenicity, limited penetration into the central nervous system, and variable transfection efficacy for skeletal muscle. Thus, the mRNA-based protein replacement represents an innovative strategy in which synthetic IVT mRNA is delivered to the patient cells to direct the synthesis of functional therapeutic proteins employing the host cellular translational machinery (Żak and Zangi, 2025). This approach offers potential advantages, including transient protein expression, avoidance of genomic integration, and flexible manufacturing. In this section, key studies of mRNA-based therapeutics for genetic disorders are presented.Considering hematological diseases, hemophilia A and hemophilia B are caused by deficiencies in factors VIII and IX, respectively (Sidonio and Malec, 2021). Preclinical studies evaluating mRNA-based therapies have been conducted to explore treatments for those disorders. For hemophilia B, an mRNA-drug encapsulated in LUNAR lipid nanoparticles (LNPs; LUNAR- a proprietary mRNA delivery platform developed by Arcturus Therapeutics, San Diego, CA, USA) encoding human factor IX (hFIX) was administered in immunocompetent hemophilic mice. High circulation levels of hFIX protein were detected after repeated administrations, demonstrating sustained protein expression (Ramaswamy et al., 2017). Similarly, studies investigating mRNA-based therapy for hemophilia A demonstrated that intravenous injection of LNP encapsulated luciferase mRNA, resulted in detectable hepatic luminescence within four hours, with no toxicity even after multiple administrations. Based on these findings, the mRNA encoding factor VIII protein was subsequently evaluated (Chen et al., 2020). This approach successfully restored biological activity, and production of therapeutic factor VIII (FVIII) protein levels was detected, above therapeutic levels, over five days. Repeated injections of FVIII-mRNA prolonged the duration of FVIII expression (Chen et al., 2020). OTC is a key enzyme in the urea cycle, a metabolic pathway responsible for ammonia detoxification. Deficiency of OTC leads to an ammonia build up in the blood (hyperammonemia), which is neurotoxic in affected individuals. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractFor nearly 50 years, scientists have sought to exploit messenger RNA (mRNA) as a therapeutic tool, overcoming major challenges related to instability, delivery, and inflammatory reactions. A major breakthrough came with the incorporation of modified nucleosides, particularly pseudouridine, during in vitro mRNA synthesis, which markedly improved stability, translation efficiency, and tolerability. The clinical success of mRNA technology was demonstrated in 2020 with the development of highly effective and safe COVID-19 vaccines, administered to over a billion individuals worldwide. These achievements inaugurated a new era in molecular medicine. In this review, we revisit the historical development of mRNA delivery into human cells and discuss the emergence of mRNA as a gene-therapy approach. In fact, beyond vaccination, mRNA platforms are rapidly expanding toward protein replacement therapies for genetic disorders and innovative strategies for cancer treatment. We summarize advances in synthetic mRNA design and optimization, delivery vehicles, and administration strategies that enable therapeutic applications. Finally, we highlight current limitations, technological challenges, and future opportunities, emphasizing how mRNA-based technologies have become powerful tools for studying gene function and developing next-generation precision therapies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to explore the development and clinical application of mRNA-based therapies, particularly in the context of rabies virus and rabies disease, highlighting the need for effective and safe treatment options.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study reviewed the historical development of mRNA delivery into human cells and discussed its emergence as a gene-therapy approach, focusing on rabies virus and rabies disease.
analysis.methods: The study described the use of lipid-based delivery systems and ionizable LNPs to introduce mRNA molecules into cells, with specific mention of in vitro-transcribed (IVT) luciferase mRNA and its application in mammalian cells.
analysis.main_results: The clinical success of mRNA-based vaccines, particularly for rabies, was demonstrated through their high efficacy and safety in protecting humans against viral pathogens, and the approval of an mRNA-based therapy for polyneuropathy associated with hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis marked the first regulatory validation of an LNP system in humans.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrated that mRNA-based therapies can safely and effectively enable systemic nucleic acid delivery, offering a promising alternative for treating genetic disorders and infectious diseases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that mRNA-based technologies can be used to develop next-generation precision therapies for rabies and other diseases, with implications for improving treatment options and expanding biomedical applications.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the development and clinical application of mRNA-based therapies, particularly in the context of rabies virus and rabies disease. It highlights the historical breakthroughs in mRNA stability and delivery, such as the use of modified nucleosides and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which have enabled the successful use of mRNA in vaccines and therapeutic applications. The study emphasizes the potential of mRNA to treat genetic disorders and infectious diseases, with specific examples including the approval of an mRNA-based therapy for polyneuropathy associated with hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis. Despite these advancements, the high costs of mRNA-based therapies have limited their widespread use. The findings demonstrate the safety and efficacy of mRNA delivery systems, providing a foundation for future research and applications in precision medicine.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究回顾了 mRNA 递送至人体细胞的历史发展,并讨论了其作为基因治疗方法的出现,重点关注 狂犬病病毒 和 狂犬病 疾病。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究描述了使用基于脂质的递送系统和可电离的 LNP 将 mRNA 分子引入细胞中,特别提到了体外转录 (IVT) 荧光素酶 mRNA 及其在哺乳动物细胞中的应用。
elements_zh.main_results: 基于 mRNA 的 疫苗,特别是 狂犬病 的临床成功,通过其在保护人类免受病毒病原体侵害方面的高效性和安全性得到了证明,基于 mRNA 的治疗与遗传性转甲状腺素蛋白介导的淀粉样变性相关的多发性神经病的批准标志着 LNP 系统在人类中的首次监管验证。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,基于 mRNA 的疗法可以安全有效地实现全身核酸输送,为治疗遗传性疾病和传染病提供了一种有前途的替代方案。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果表明,基于 mRNA 的技术可用于开发针对 狂犬病 和其他疾病的下一代精准疗法,这对改善 治疗 选择和扩大生物医学应用具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究指出,基于 mRNA 的疗法的高成本限制了其广泛的临床应用,尽管有充分的证据证明其有效性和安全性,但仍需要进一步研究来解决技术挑战并提高可及性。

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究回顾了 mRNA 递送至人体细胞的历史发展,并讨论了其作为基因治疗方法的出现,重点关注 狂犬病病毒 和 狂犬病 疾病。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究描述了使用基于脂质的递送系统和可电离的 LNP 将 mRNA 分子引入细胞中,特别提到了体外转录 (IVT) 荧光素酶 mRNA 及其在哺乳动物细胞中的应用。
analysis_zh.main_results: 基于 mRNA 的 疫苗,特别是 狂犬病 的临床成功,通过其在保护人类免受病毒病原体侵害方面的高效性和安全性得到了证明,基于 mRNA 的治疗与遗传性转甲状腺素蛋白介导的淀粉样变性相关的多发性神经病的批准标志着 LNP 系统在人类中的首次监管验证。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,基于 mRNA 的疗法可以安全有效地实现全身核酸输送,为治疗遗传性疾病和传染病提供了一种有前途的替代方案。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果表明,基于 mRNA 的技术可用于开发针对 狂犬病 和其他疾病的下一代精准疗法,这对改善 治疗 选择和扩大生物医学应用具有重要意义。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究指出,基于 mRNA 的疗法的高成本限制了其广泛的临床应用,尽管有充分的证据证明其有效性和安全性,但仍需要进一步研究来解决技术挑战并提高可及性。

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTIntroductionZoonotic diseases pose risks to human, animal, and ecosystem health; effective management relies on coordinated actions across sectors. Although One Health principles promote collaboration across sectors, operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment (RA) are lacking. Therefore, the Tripartite (FAO, WHO, and WOAH) developed the first‐ever One Health operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA‐OT), with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. This article describes how information from pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia contributed to informing co‐development of the final JRA process and tool.MethodsThree in‐person meetings with international RA and zoonotic disease experts with a One Health background were convened in Rome, Italy, to co‐develop the methodology (November 2017, September 2018) and incorporate pilot feedback (February 2020). Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. The pilot workshops described here were conducted in Indonesia (March 2018), the United Republic of Tanzania (March 2019), and Georgia (July 2019), and feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat.ResultsThese pilot workshops demonstrated JRA's utility and provided critical information for improvements. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. The process serves as a model for co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools.Keywords: Joint Operational Tools, One Health, risk assessment, zoonoses Piloting of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) process and tool in countries provided feedback for improvement, evidence‐based estimates of national risks from priority zoonotic diseases, and practical training of national facilitators. The JRA offers simple step‐by‐step guidance to countries wishing to undertake joint qualitative risk assessments. 2.Methods2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. They reviewed and examined existing sector‐specific RA methods and tools for their suitability and relevance and agreed on the following criteria for the joint RA: Provide a standard, systematic process for conducting evidence‐based RA on joint priority zoonotic disease hazards.Be qualitative and facilitate incorporation of expert opinion when only minimal and/or poor‐quality data are available.Allow identification of data gaps, and benefit from iterative use as additional data becomes available.Promote use of data and results from sector‐specific RAs.Provide step‐by‐step operational guidance to facilitate effective and equitable collaboration and sharing of information, expertise, and perspectives.Be prospectively joint across all relevant sectors, that is, public health (e.g., ministries of health, public health agencies), animal health (e.g., veterinary services), environmental (e.g., wildlife health, environmental protection agencies), and others, such as security and disaster services.Function within existing zoonotic disease management and One Health governance infrastructures.Be adaptable to the relevant contextBe usable by governments, academia, or anyone wishing to conduct RA jointly across sectors.Support international sector‐specific RA and health security frameworks (e.g., International Health Regulations [9], WHO Rapid RA [4], WOAH Import Risk Analysis [5], FAO draft Guidelines on Rapid RA [now published [6]]).Once the new basic JRA process and tool were agreed, they were tested during (1) two international in‐person workshops in Rome, Italy (November 2017, September 2018), bringing together international multisectoral RA experts from different geographical regions selected by the three organizations to review and fine‐tune the methodology, and (2) 15 country pilots conducted between March 2018 and December 2019 (Figure 1), which guided iterative updates. All pilots were in‐person and had the same direct and indirect objectives (Table 1). A final in‐person expert consultation was held in Rome, Italy (February 2020), and the JRA‐OT was published in December 2020 [8]. The development timeline is depicted in Figure 2.FIGURE 1Joint Risk Assessment pilot countries.TABLE 1Objectives of the Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) pilot workshops.Direct objectivesIndirect objectives Build capacity through training a pool of national facilitators to operationalize the JRA tool at national and subnational levelsProvide likelihood and impact estimates for risk assessment questions on priority hazardsAssess the usefulness of the JRA and consider its sustained useCollect feedback to improve interim versions of the JRA Enhance coordination and trust among relevant stakeholdersFacilitate official and unofficial communication and information sharing among stakeholdersAdvocate for allocation of resources FIGURE 2Development timeline of the Joint Risk Assessment operational tool.2.2.Pilot WorkshopsFor each of the 15 pilot workshops, all relevant ministries, particularly those responsible for animal health and public health, were encouraged to engage through outreach by FAO and WHO country offices. Tripartite central, regional, and country office staff supported the workshops as external facilitators. All pilots, aside from the Indonesian pilot where the risk framing was conducted during the workshop, followed the six steps, below and in Figure 3, adapted from common RA processes used in public health, animal health, and/or environmental RA: Hazard identification: Technical staff and decision‐makers in engaged ministries (hereafter, “ministries”) agreed on national priority endemic, epidemic, or emerging zoonotic hazards, up to 6 months prior to the workshop. Risk framing: Once the hazards were agreed, ministerial decision‐makers characterized the scope, purpose, and objectives of the assessment on the basis of government strategy and policy to ensure the JRA process remained efficient and focused on critical government needs. Selection of participants and national staff: After Steps 1 and 2, ministries identified participants based on the identified hazards and risk framing and selected staff to facilitate the planning and implementation of the pilot and future JRAs (hereafter, “national facilitators”). A JRA lead was agreed among ministries. High‐level ministerial participation was encouraged for workshop Days 0 and 3. Day 0: National facilitators finalized the risk framing and were trained on the JRA process and tool by the external facilitators. Days 1–2: The JRA was introduced and undertaken by participants, led by the national facilitators and supported by external facilitators. Small groups each focused on one identified hazard using information brought to the workshop and presented the outcome of each step in plenary. Substantial time was dedicated to plenary discussion and questions, covering both the technical assessments and the JRA process itself. Day 3: Each group presented final results in plenary. Participants, including decision‐makers, considered existing national zoonotic disease and One Health infrastructure and options for governance of routine JRA leadership and implementation, and identified what criteria would trigger conducting or updating a JRA.FIGURE 3Schematic of the final Joint Risk Assessment process applied during national JRA pilots. Steps are fully described in WHO et al. [8].2.3.Data Capture, Analysis, and IntegrationFrom each pilot's planning period through to the end of each workshop, constraints, challenges, and proposed solutions gleaned from plenary and group workshop discussions, and verbal feedback from participants and national facilitators were captured in written notes taken by the external facilitators. Standardized written feedback on the process, tool, and workshop was requested anonymously from attendees using a questionnaire (Pilot Feedback Form; see Supporting Information). Completion of questionnaires was optional.At the end of each workshop day, the external and national facilitators gathered to discuss how the day went and share the feedback received so far. Potential modifications to the JRA based on captured information and challenges were continually discussed among the pilot facilitators and the Tripartite focal points leading the development of the JRA (hereafter, JRA Secretariat). After each pilot workshop, the JRA Secretariat met virtually to revisit the feedback received and suggest corrective actions to the tool and process accordingly. On the basis of importance, urgency, and complexity, straightforward and uncontroversial corrections were made by the JRA Secretariat immediately and prior to the next workshop, whereas more complex issues were collected in a list of discussion points and brought forward to expert review and decision during the final expert workshop held in Rome (September 2018). As pilots were conducted, the JRA Secretariat noted that challenges fell into three categories: Challenges that were consistent across countries, such as misleading or unclear text, and definitely required changing to ensure comprehension.Challenges that varied across countries and could not be improved in a generic way and were best managed by stating in JRA materials that these aspects are country‐specific and would be managed during national JRAs.Challenges that fell outside the scope of the JRA process and would not be useful to address in the tool.2.4.Country Pilot Selection for This ManuscriptThe pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia (Table 2 and further described chronologically below) were purposively selected by the JRA Secretariat for further description in this manuscript, based on (1) each being the first country in its geographical region to conduct a JRA pilot and (2) the level of contribution the country's findings had in informing the final JRA content and processes.TABLE 2Summary of Joint Risk Assessment pilot workshops in Indonesia, Tanzania, and Georgia.IndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaDatesMarch 13–16, 2018March 25–28, 2019July 2–5, 2019LocationBogorDar es SalaamKakhetiNumber of participants642425Hazards assessedZoonotic influenza viruses, rabies virus, Leptospira interrogans Zoonotic influenza viruses, rabies virus, Bacillus anthracis Rabies virus, Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus Supplementary Materials Supporting File: puh270398‐sup‐0001‐SuppMat.pdf. 3.Results3.1.IndonesiaThe Indonesian JRA pilot workshop was the first JRA pilot conducted and took place in Bogor on March 13–16, 2018. The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces. Five hazards (zoonotic influenza viruses in three different contexts, rabies virus, and Leptospira interrogans) were assessed. Leveraging the strong multisectoral engagement and zoonotic disease experience of local partners facilitated the emergence of important lessons. Because Indonesia was the first pilot, these lessons greatly impacted the JRA process and tool and all subsequent pilots.The Indonesia pilot generated key findings related to risk framing, pre‐workshop training, political will, and subnational involvement.3.1.1.Introducing a Risk‐Framing StepInitially, the draft JRA process did not include a step where decision‐makers could provide strategic and policy‐related inputs to frame the assessment. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. The national facilitators suggested that ministerial decision‐makers could undertake this step prior to the workshop, inspiring the addition of the pre‐pilot risk‐framing step to the final JRA.3.1.2.Adding a 1‐Day Pre‐Workshop Training for National FacilitatorsInitially, the “Day 0 national facilitators” training was also not part of the JRA process. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. Skilled national facilitators would not only bring local context and perspectives but also create JRA sustainability, as external facilitators would no longer be needed for subsequent national and subnational JRAs. Subsequently, “Day 0” was incorporated for all future pilots, with national facilitators and JRA Secretariat attending Days 0–3 and all other participants attending Days 1–3. “Day 0” is not included in the tool as the JRA is meant to be done autonomously by countries, that is, once facilitators are familiar with the JRA tool and process.3.1.3.Importance of Political Will for JRA SuccessThe Government of Indonesia (GOI) was the first government to request a JRA workshop in 2017. The Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (Kemenko PMK) were strongly involved in planning and implementation. Director‐level representatives from these agencies were present during the entire workshop, contributed operationally to discussions, and were available to support the unanticipated risk‐framing activity. Not only did the Director General of MoH Prevention and Disease Control open the JRA, but he also requested a side meeting with the JRA Secretariat to show his direct support and appreciation of the JRA initiative and One Health approaches in general. The team agreed that this high‐level political engagement, as well as leveraging the strong national One Health culture, facilitated the later implementation of JRAs at national and subnational levels [10, 11]. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. Both Tanzania's experience managing zoonotic diseases and the active OHCD for multisectoral coordination, which had experience organizing One Health trainings, facilitated success in pre‐pilot activities and workshop planning.The Tanzania pilot validated key findings from the Indon…

As pilots were conducted, the JRA Secretariat noted that challenges fell into three categories: Challenges that were consistent across countries, such as misleading or unclear text, and definitely required changing to ensure comprehension.Challenges that varied across countries and could not be improved in a generic way and were best managed by stating in JRA materials that these aspects are country‐specific and would be managed during national JRAs.Challenges that fell outside the scope of the JRA process and would not be useful to address in the tool.2.4.Country Pilot Selection for This ManuscriptThe pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia (Table 2 and further described chronologically below) were purposively selected by the JRA Secretariat for further description in this manuscript, based on…
full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.IndonesiaThe Indonesian JRA pilot workshop was the first JRA pilot conducted and took place in Bogor on March 13–16, 2018. The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces. Five hazards (zoonotic influenza viruses in three different contexts, rabies virus, and Leptospira interrogans) were assessed. Leveraging the strong multisectoral engagement and zoonotic disease experience of local partners facilitated the emergence of important lessons. Because Indonesia was the first pilot, these lessons greatly impacted the JRA process and tool and all subsequent pilots.The Indonesia pilot generated key findings related to risk framing, pre‐workshop training, political will, and subnational involvement.3.1.1.Introducing a Risk‐Framing StepInitially, the draft JRA process did not include a step where decision‐makers could provide strategic and policy‐related inputs to frame the assessment. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. The national facilitators suggested that ministerial decision‐makers could undertake this step prior to the workshop, inspiring the addition of the pre‐pilot risk‐framing step to the final JRA.3.1.2.Adding a 1‐Day Pre‐Workshop Training for National FacilitatorsInitially, the “Day 0 national facilitators” training was also not part of the JRA process. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. Skilled national facilitators would not only bring local context and perspectives but also create JRA sustainability, as external facilitators would no longer be needed for subsequent national and subnational JRAs. Subsequently, “Day 0” was incorporated for all future pilots, with national facilitators and JRA Secretariat attending Days 0–3 and all other participants attending Days 1–3. “Day 0” is not included in the tool as the JRA is meant to be done autonomously by countries, that is, once facilitators are familiar with the JRA tool and process.3.1.3.Importance of Political Will for JRA SuccessThe Government of Indonesia (GOI) was the first government to request a JRA workshop in 2017. The Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (Kemenko PMK) were strongly involved in planning and implementation. Director‐level representatives from these agencies were present during the entire workshop, contributed operationally to discussions, and were available to support the unanticipated risk‐framing activity. Not only did the Director General of MoH Prevention and Disease Control open the JRA, but he also requested a side meeting with the JRA Secretariat to show his direct support and appreciation of the JRA initiative and One Health approaches in general. The team agreed that this high‐level political engagement, as well as leveraging the strong national One Health culture, facilitated the later implementation of JRAs at national and subnational levels [10, 11]. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. Both Tanzania's experience managing zoonotic diseases and the active OHCD for multisectoral coordination, which had experience organizing One Health trainings, facilitated success in pre‐pilot activities and workshop planning.The Tanzania pilot validated key findings from the Indonesia pilot. As with Indonesia, Tanzanian participants suggested organizing nationally led ToT at the central and subnational levels. The importance of political will and high‐level input was affirmed, with ministerial participation on all 4 days of the workshop. Zanzibar was highlighted as a priority setting for implementing subnational JRAs, confirming their importance and value. Further findings included the use of virtual risk framing and using existing structures to sustain JRA implementation.3.2.1.Risk Framing Through Virtual ConsultationTanzania was one of the first countries to conduct a risk framing and the first done virtually with support from the JRA Secretariat. Practical lessons were learned about risk‐framing implementation, for example, that each hazard should be framed separately, and that the risk‐framing template should contain only information strictly necessary to focus the RA. Importantly, Tanzania demonstrated that the risk framing was effectively done virtually, and benefits of the virtual risk‐framing meeting were noted by the JRA Secretariat.3.2.2.Utilizing the Existing Multisectoral Coordination Mechanism as JRA Steering CommitteeAlready in 2015, Tanzania had developed and implemented its Prime Ministerial level One Health Strategic Plan and had establ…
full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionTo address the lack of One Health operational tools to guide joint, multisectoral RA for zoonotic disease threats, the Tripartite co‐developed the JRA‐OT with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. Between 2015 and 2020, feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat to generate the final version [8] published in 2020.Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia were the first to be conducted in their respective geographical regions and generated key lessons that were particularly important for informing the final tool and, thus, were selected for detailed description in this manuscript. There was much overlap across the findings from these countries, suggesting that they also represented countries generally. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culture from the three countries, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) inclusion of all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and ToTs (Table 3).TABLE 3Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed across pilots and integrated into the final Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) tool and process.Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed through JRA pilotsLesson learned inIndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaValue of policy‐level risk framing (in person or online)xxxImportance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culturexxxNeed for subnational engagementxxxImportance of including all relevant sectorsxNecessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and training of trainersxx4.1.Value of Policy‐Level Risk FramingOne of the most important findings across pilots was the need for a formal risk‐framing process led by decision‐makers ahead of the workshop. In Indonesia, participants realized that defining the scope, objectives, and policy priorities during the workshop itself was inefficient and only possible because senior officials were present. Tanzania further demonstrated that risk framing could be conducted effectively through virtual consultations and highlighted the importance of framing each hazard separately. In Georgia, better aligning the hazards and framing with national priorities related to tourism and trade on Day 0 reinforced the importance of strong policy input in hazard selection and framing prior to the workshop.4.2.Importance of Political Will and Leveraging Existing One Health CultureAll three pilots showed that high‐level political commitment and existing multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms were critical for successful implementation, as proposed by Yopa et al. [14]. Indonesia benefited from strong ministerial engagement and an established One Health governance structure, which later supported national and provincial JRA expansion. Tanzania's politically supported OHCD played a central role in organizing and sustaining JRA activities, whereas ministerial participation throughout the workshop reinforced national ownership. Similarly, Georgia's existing One Health Division within the NCDC facilitated planning, coordination, and policy relevance. Across pilots, political support increased participant engagement, improved alignment with national priorities, and facilitated translating JRA findings into action.4.3.Need for Subnational EngagementThe pilots consistently demonstrated that involving subnational participants improved the relevance and practicality of assessments. During pilots, subnational participants were noted to be especially engaged and motivated to act. In Indonesia, representatives from three provinces assessed influenza risks in their own local contexts, enabling development of tailored risk management strategies and demonstrating that zoonotic risks are often context‐specific rather than purely national. Tanzania identified Zanzibar as a priority setting for future subnational JRAs, highlighting the value of localized implementation. In Georgia, regional participants emphasized differences in rabies epidemiology across areas and proposed immediate use of JRA methods at the subnational level. Overall, the pilots showed that subnational participation strengthens contextual understanding, improves local ownership, and supports implementation of locally relevant mitigation measures.4.4.Inclusion of all Relevant SectorsAnother key lesson was the importance of ensuring representation from all relevant sectors in JRA workshops. Georgia particularly illustrated this challenge when the absence of the wildlife sector limited discussions on rabies risks involving wildlife transmission. This experience demonstrated that gaps in sectoral participation can reduce the completeness and quality of assessments. However, it also showed that the JRA process itself can help identify missing stakeholders and strengthen multisectoral collaboration over time. Across pilots, broad participation from human health, animal health, environment, disaster management, and other sectors was recognized as essential for comprehensive RA and effective One Health coordination for zoonotic diseases.4.5.Necessity of Clear, Stepwise Operational Guidance, and ToTsThe pilots highlighted the need for practical, stepwise operational guidance and strong national facilitation capacity. Indonesia pioneered the Day 0 national facilitator training, which became a standard feature of subsequent JRAs. This training helped facilitators understand the methodology, practice facilitation skills, and eventually lead workshops independently, reducing reliance on external experts. Pilots in Tanzania and Georgia validated the value of this approach, with national facilitators increasingly taking ownership of workshop implementation. The Georgia pilot highlighted the need for clearer guidance on hazard selection and joint risk‐framing procedures that were then added into the tool. In both Indonesia and Tanzania, participants recommended national and subnational ToT programs to build sustainable in‐country expertise. Together, these experiences emphasized that successful JRA implementation depends not only on the tool itself, but also on clear, stepwise operational guidance, standardized processes, and national capacity building.After review and discussion of these key lessons learned, the JRA Secretariat made the following revisions to the JRA tool and process: (1) introduction of a dedicated pre‐workshop risk‐framing Step 2 in the JRA process, led by decision‐makers, including a template for framing risks related to each hazard identified in Step 1; (2) highlighting the importance of political will and the opportunity to leverage existing national One Health structures to sustainably implement JRA; and (3) highlighting the importance of prospective inclusion of all relevant sectors, with participation of national and subnational levels, especially relevant in Step 3 where participants are being identified. The full‐day training for national facilitators on Day 0 was added to planning for all future workshops to foster ownership in country pilots, familiarize national facilitators, including subnational staff, with the JRA steps and some basic facilitation principles and review the workshop objectives.All three countries saw the JRA as an opportunity to operationalize One Health strategies while producing practical, tangible outputs, specifically, consolidated hazard information, qualitative risk estimates, and options for risk‐based management and communication.The evidence‐based JRA output served as advocacy to secure high‐level commitment and resources for risk mitigation. Participants from different sectors often still did not know each other, despite ongoing multisectoral activities and high levels of One Health awareness further emphasized the need to strengthen routine collaborative activities, such as JRA.The JRA process can present challenges. Without strong One Health leader…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionKnowledge iteratively gained during pilots was critical to enhance the usefulness and effectiveness of the JRA process and tool, and ownership by different sectors. Key lessons can be grouped into the following categories: The value of policy‐level risk framingThe importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health structuresThe need for subnational engagementThe importance of all relevant sectors being engaged and presentThe need for clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainersThe JRA pilots demonstrated that effective zoonotic disease RA requires strong integration of technical analysis with policy‐level decision‐making, particularly through early and structured risk framing. Sustained political commitment and established One Health coordination mechanisms were critical enablers of successful JRA implementation and long‐term national ownership. Inclusion of subnational actors and all relevant sectors significantly improved the contextual relevance, completeness, and operational value of RAs.The pilots showed that JRAs can serve not only as technical tools for RA, but also as mechanisms for strengthening multisectoral collaboration, information sharing, and One Health governance. Standardized operational guidance, facilitator training, and nationally led ToTs were essential for building sustainable country capacity and reducing reliance on external support.The JRA was co‐developed iteratively and inclusively across countries, sectors, and scales to meet objectives laid down by national governments and experts in RA and zoonotic diseases to assess risks, and thus models One Health best practice in both content and process and ensures ownership by the different sectors. The methodology can be used as a model for development of other multisectoral operational processes and tools. The JRA's inclusive, systematic, and evidence‐based RA process is now available to all countries, improving management of critical national zoonotic disease risks.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionActions and policies to identify, assess, manage, and reduce risks from zoonotic diseases benefit from functional collaboration and engagement across stakeholders and sectors, including academia, the private sector, local communities, and government ministries responsible for human health, animal health, food safety, wildlife, environment, trade, education, security and disasters, and the economy [1]. Under the International Health Regulations (2005) monitoring and evaluation framework—Joint External Evaluation guidance [2], countries should have the capacity to conduct joint assessments of risk for zoonotic diseases using a One Health approach.In 2014, countries concerned about the potential spread of a zoonotic avian influenza A(H7N9) virus strain in Asia wished to align the results of sectoral risk assessments (RAs) and risk‐related communication messages but encountered challenges in sharing information and conducting RA jointly across sectors. Due to its sensitive nature, information related to zoonotic diseases can potentially influence consumer behavior and/or compromise a country's economy or tourism if made public. Sharing such information between sectors often must be authorized and may be restricted or delayed, especially in the absence of clear sharing mechanisms or policies. Further, although countries could access sector‐specific RA methodologies and processes, they encountered challenges in assessing risks jointly when encountering differing steps and terminology across RA methods and the reluctance of sectors to agree on an approach unfamiliar to them in the absence of expert guidance. These countries requested assistance from the Tripartite [3] to identify and propose a technically sound approach to conducting joint, multisectoral zoonotic disease RA.Technical aspects of estimating risks are, in principle, similar across RA methods, and it is normally possible to incorporate information from other sectors during sector‐specific zoonotic disease RAs. However, each sector‐specific method evolved to achieve different objectives. Consequently, RA methods are operationally different, do not easily align, and do not lend themselves to joint use. Although many institutions and agencies publish RA reports for zoonotic diseases, an extensive search of published guidance for conducting zoonotic disease RA across health‐related disciplines identified only sector‐specific tools available at that time. Further, the guidance from WHO [4], WOAH [5](updated in 2024) and FAO [6](available internally but unpublished at the time) referred to assessment for zoonotic diseases but had been developed exclusively by and for the human health and animal health sectors, respectively. The RA procedures of the Codex Alimentarius Commission [7] were also available but primarily focused on quantitative assessment of contaminants in food and were not practical for use by countries. To fill this gap, the Tripartite convened international RA experts and pilot countries to iteratively co‐develop the first‐ever One Health operational tool for conducting zoonotic disease RA jointly across sectors.The Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) was published as the Joint Risk Assessment Operational Tool (JRA‐OT) in 2020 [8], as one of the operational tools supporting the Tripartite Zoonoses Guide [1]. The JRA‐OT provides a systematic and iterative step‐by‐step process to bring together stakeholders from different sectors. Together, they share expertise, discuss available information, and jointly identify and qualitatively assess risks associated with zoonotic hazards nationally and subnationally, based on strategic policy concerns. Benefits include the following: Facilitates sharing of information and expertise from all relevant sectors, increasing the technical validity of results, including evidence‐based management measures and communication messages.Facilitates agreement and ownership of results across sectors, allowing development of nuanced and acceptable management interventions with fewer negative externalities.Prospectively considers strategic policy needs across sectors at national and subnational levels, expediting aligned and contextualized implementation done jointly or separately by each sector.Fosters mutual understanding of perceptions, mandates, constraints, and daily work across sectors, improving communication for future collaborative activities, including emergency response.Identifies missing information, allowing targeting of surveillance, research, and capacity building.Facilitates political engagement and support for sustained One Health collaboration through establishment of a routine technical, output‐driven collaborative process located within a multisectoral coordination and governance infrastructure.This article describes the iterative and collaborative process undertaken to co‐develop the JRA, which is an example of and a model for applied One Health, demonstrating: Initiation based on needs of the user communityBalanced, shared leadership across multiple sectorsInclusion of expertise, perspectives, information, and experiences from across a broad, inclusive, and multi‐scalar scope of technical and policy stakeholdersIterative consideration and integration of knowledge insights acquired during implementationThe JRA itself exemplifies best practices in One Health implementation, namely, Developing a shared objectiveUsing a standardized process to facilitate collaboration, reduce conflict, and achieve joint outputsProviding tangible outputs, specifically, consolidated hazard information, qualitative risk estimates, and options for risk‐based management and communication, that are immediately practical, relevant to local contexts, and useful for diverse stakeholdersBuilding technical capacityDemonstrating transparency and inclusivityPromoting trust, awareness, and relationship‐building across sectors and scalesHere we describe national pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia, selected on the basis of their importance in informing the final JRA process and tool. Our findings serve as a model to inform co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools by applying an inclusive and consultative process consistent with the One Health approach. 2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. papers.title_original: Iterative Co‐Development of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment Operational Process and Tool Through Incorporating Information From Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop an operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) to manage zoonotic diseases, as effective multisectoral risk assessment is critical for addressing health risks across human, animal, and ecosystem sectors.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved pilot workshops in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia, conducted between March 2018 and December 2019. These workshops included 64 participants from central government ministries and subnational staff across human and animal health, forestry, security, and disaster sectors.
analysis.methods: The JRA process was developed through iterative co-development with country pilots and international experts. Existing sector-specific risk assessment methods were reviewed for suitability, and standardized feedback forms were used to collect anonymous input from participants.
analysis.main_results: The pilot workshops demonstrated the utility of the JRA process and provided critical feedback for its improvement. Key findings included the value of policy-level risk framing, the importance of political will, the need for subnational engagement, and the necessity of clear, stepwise guidance for efficient collaboration.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of the JRA process's effectiveness in facilitating multisectoral collaboration and improving risk assessment tools. The novelty lies in the co-development approach that integrates stakeholder feedback and expert input into a standardized, operational framework.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment, supporting more effective and equitable collaboration across public health, animal health, and environmental sectors in managing zoonotic diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on feedback from pilot workshops, which may not fully represent broader contexts. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on qualitative feedback and iterative improvements rather than quantitative data.

analysis.summary_en: This study describes the development and testing of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) operational tool through pilot workshops in Indonesia, Tanzania, and Georgia. The JRA process was designed to be a standard, systematic, and qualitative method for assessing joint priority zoonotic disease hazards, incorporating expert opinion and sector-specific risk assessments. The pilot workshops highlighted the importance of policy-level risk framing, political will, subnational engagement, and clear guidance for effective collaboration. The findings suggest that the JRA tool can support multisectoral risk assessment and training, but the evidence is based on qualitative feedback and iterative improvements, limiting its strength. The study contributes to the field by demonstrating the feasibility of co-developing operational tools for zoonotic disease risk management.

analysis_en.methods: The JRA process was developed through iterative co-development with country pilots and international experts. Existing sector-specific risk assessment methods were reviewed for suitability, and standardized feedback forms were used to collect anonymous input from participants.
analysis_en.main_results: The pilot workshops demonstrated the utility of the JRA process and provided critical feedback for its improvement. Key findings included the value of policy-level risk framing, the importance of political will, the need for subnational engagement, and the necessity of clear, stepwise guidance for efficient collaboration.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of the JRA process's effectiveness in facilitating multisectoral collaboration and improving risk assessment tools. The novelty lies in the co-development approach that integrates stakeholder feedback and expert input into a standardized, operational framework.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment, supporting more effective and equitable collaboration across public health, animal health, and environmental sectors in managing zoonotic diseases.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on feedback from pilot workshops, which may not fully represent broader contexts. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on qualitative feedback and iterative improvements rather than quantitative data.

papers.title_zh: 通过纳入印度尼西亚、坦桑尼亚联合共和国和格鲁吉亚试点的信息,迭代共同开发三方联合风险评估操作流程和工具
papers.source_body_en: Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. papers.abstract_zh: 制定标准包括标准、系统、定性和多部门的风险评估流程,促进纳入专家意见和特定部门的风险评估结果。主要发现包括 (1) 政策层面风险框架的价值,(2) 政治意愿的重要性,(3) 地方参与的必要性,(4) 包括所有相关部门的重要性,以及 (5) 明确、逐步的指导的必要性,以促进高效合作和支持国家培训师的培训。对国家人畜共患疾病风险的多部门评估以及不同部门的所有权。他们审查和检查了现有的特定部门风险评估方法和工具的适用性和相关性,并就联合风险评估的以下标准达成一致:提供一个标准、系统的流程,用于对联合优先的人畜共患疾病危害进行基于证据的风险评估。当只有很少和/或质量较差的数据时,要定性并促进纳入专家意见。允许识别数据差距,并在获得更多数据时从迭代使用中受益。促进使用特定部门风险评估的数据和结果。提供逐步的操作指导,以促进有效和公平的合作以及信息、专业知识和观点的共享。前瞻性地联合所有相关部门,即公共卫生(例如卫生部、公共卫生机构)、动物健康(例如兽医服务)、环境(例如野生动物健康、环境保护机构)以及其他部门,例如安全和卫生部门。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在开发一种联合风险评估(JRA)的操作工具来管理人畜共患疾病,因为有效的多部门风险评估对于解决人类、动物和生态系统部门的健康风险至关重要。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究于 2018 年 3 月至 2019 年 12 月期间在印度尼西亚、坦桑尼亚联合共和国和格鲁吉亚举办了试点研讨会。这些研讨会有 64 名来自中央政府部委以及人类和动物健康、林业、安全和灾害部门的地方工作人员参加。
analysis_zh.methods: JRA 流程是通过与国家试点和国际专家反复共同开发而制定的。对现有特定部门风险评估方法的适用性进行了审查,并使用标准化反馈表收集参与者的匿名意见。
analysis_zh.main_results: 试点研讨会展示了 JRA 流程的实用性,并为其改进提供了重要的反馈。主要调查结果包括政策层面风险框架的价值、政治意愿的重要性、地方参与的必要性以及有效合作的明确、逐步指导的必要性。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为 JRA 流程在促进多部门合作和改进风险评估工具方面的有效性的证据。新颖之处在于共同开发方法,它将利益相关者的反馈和专家的意见整合到标准化的操作框架中。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为多部门风险评估操作工具的开发提供了信息,支持公共卫生、动物健康和环境部门在管理人畜共患疾病方面进行更有效和公平的合作。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于它依赖于试点研讨会的反馈,而这些反馈可能无法完全代表更广泛的背景。证据是中等的,因为它基于定性反馈和迭代改进而不是定量数据。

papers.title: Dopamine release-associated striatal blood oxygenation and whole-brain dynamics during associative learning

source_records.title: Dopamine release-associated striatal blood oxygenation and whole-brain dynamics during associative learning
