papers.full_text: AbstractBackgroundFree-roaming cats (Felis catus) in urban environments are commonly managed through trap–neuter–return (TNR) programs, yet the long-term population effects of these measures remain inconsistently evaluated, particularly when considering both population size and structural dynamics.ObjectivesThis study aimed to assess long-term changes in free-roaming cat populations and population-structure patterns observed in the context of public TNR program in Seoul, Republic of Korea, using multiple demographic and structural indicators, specifically neutering rate, kitten proportion, and apparent retention.MethodsA longitudinal observational study was conducted across 17 fixed survey sites from 2017 to 2025. Repeated field surveys were performed biennially, with at least five visits per site. Population size, neutering rate, kitten proportion, and apparent retention were calculated via non-invasive photographic individual identification. Negative binomial and binomial mixed-effects models evaluated temporal trends and land-use differences. A logistic mixed effects model assessed apparent retention by baseline neutering status, and within-year encounter histories were used to estimate detection probability.ResultsOverall population size and density showed a decreasing temporal pattern, while neutering rates generally increased and kitten proportions generally decreased. At the survey-year level, higher neutering rates coincided with lower kitten proportions. After adjustment for covariates and site-level clustering, cats neutered at baseline had significantly higher odds of apparent retention than non-neutered cats (OR = 3.06, 95% CI: 2.07–4.53). The pooled single-visit detection probability was 0.299, indicating that apparent retention remained subject to imperfect detection. In exploratory site-level comparisons, sites maintaining high neutering rates showed patterns consistent with lower kitten proportions and higher apparent retention, whereas sites with declining neutering rates showed patterns consistent with greater apparent turnover and higher kitten proportions.ConclusionsThese findings describe population-structure patterns observed during implementation of Seoul's public TNR program, including reduced kitten counts and increased neutering probability over time. Given the observational nature of the study and the absence of untreated controls, these findings cannot demonstrate the causal effects of TNR. Nevertheless, structural indicators may complement simple procedure counts to identify sites requiring further intervention in urban cat management.Keywords: free-roaming cats, kitten proportion, longitudinal study, neutering rate, population dynamics, population structure, trap-neuter-return, urban ecology 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study area, policy context, and study designThis study was conducted as a longitudinal observational evaluation of the population status and structural characteristics of free-roaming cats in Seoul, Republic of Korea. Seoul is a high-density metropolitan city with an area of approximately 605.6 km2, and a population exceeding 9.5 million. The city comprises heterogeneous land-use types, including residential, commercial, industrial, and green areas. This heterogeneity may influence the distribution, density, and movement patterns of free-roaming cats.Since 2008, the Seoul Metropolitan Government has implemented a publicly funded TNR program, operating a complaint-driven TNR system across 25 administrative districts. Under this program, cats are captured following citizen reports, surgically sterilized, and returned to their original locations; ear-tipping is routinely performed to enable visual identification of neutered individuals, and vaccination against rabies has been included as part of the protocol since 2023. Caregivers or local residents may participate in trapping and release, and the program has been implemented as a one-stop process coordinated by local governments. This policy framework provides a basis for evaluating long-term changes in urban free-roaming cat populations through repeated observations. However, the present study was not intended to evaluate TNR in isolation. Seoul's free-roaming cat population dynamics may also have been influenced by broader urban management and human-associated factors, including shelter capacity, impoundment and shelter-intake practices, adoption systems, caregiver activity, intentional feeding, food-waste access and garbage management, abandonment, and local community responses to cats. Because standardized site-level and year-specific data on these factors were not available across all survey sites and years, they were treated as contextual factors and potential confounders but were not incorporated as covariates in the main longitudinal analyses.The primary longitudinal surveys were performed biennially from 2017 to 2025 at 17 fixed survey sites. A preliminary exploratory survey was conducted in 2015 at nine sites to assess field feasibility and inform the subsequent sampling framework; however, these 2015 data were not included in the primary longitudinal analyses because the full 17-site design was implemented from 2017 onward. Each survey year was conducted between mid-September and October, the period when individuals born during the breeding season reach the juvenile stage, allowing simultaneous observation of both reproductive outcomes and the adult population.2.2.Study sites and sampling frameworkStudy sites were selected based on land-use classifications defined under the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, and included four categories: residential, commercial, semi-industrial, and green areas (28). Site allocation was designed so as to broadly reflect the distribution of land-use types in Seoul, where residential areas account for the largest proportion, followed by green areas, with relatively smaller proportions of commercial and semi-industrial zones. Accordingly, more sites were assigned to residential areas (n = 11), while fewer sites were included for other land-use types (n = 2 each).Site selection was informed by 2016 Seoul TNR implementation data. TNR density (cases per km2) was calculated at the administrative district level, and sites with densities approximating the citywide average (21.29 cases/km2) were preferentially selected to avoid overrepresentation of extreme conditions. This site-selection strategy was intended to improve comparability among survey sites, but it also narrowed the range of baseline intervention intensity available for analysis and may have attenuated the ability to detect dose–response relationships between TNR intensity and population outcomes.Green areas were limited to urban parks and accessible green spaces, but excluded mountainous regions, to ensure comparability with other urban environments. Candidate sites within each land-use category were identified using map-based screening to match a standardized survey area (approximately 70,000–100,000 m2), corresponding to the area that could be systematically surveyed on foot within approximately 4 h. At two sites, the survey boundaries were modestly expanded from 2021 to include immediately adjacent areas in response to redevelopment; the monitoring locality, land-use classification, survey effort, and field procedures remained unchanged.This approach was designed to capture structurally representative urban environments while ensuring the feasibility of repeated surveys and comparability of spatial coverage for longitudinal analysis, as opposed to a random sampling approach. A preliminary exploratory survey was conducted across nine sites in 2015 to assess field feasibility and inform the subsequent sampling framework. From 2017 onward, the survey design was restructured to include 17 fixed sites in order to better reflect land-use representation. Longitudinal analyses in this study were primarily based on data collected between 2017 and 2025, during which the study design remained consistent. The 2015 data were not included in the primary analytical dataset. Detailed site information is provided in Supplementary Table 1.2.3.Field survey and individual identificationField surveys were conducted at each site at least 5 times per survey year. Each survey lasted approximately 4 h and was carried out before sunset. Because surveys were conducted before sunset, the dataset primarily reflects cats visible during late daytime or crepuscular survey periods rather than the full 24-h activity cycle. This timing was kept consistent across survey years to improve comparability of repeated observations. Observers systematically traversed roads, alleys, and pedestrian pathways within each site to ensure comprehensive spatial coverage.Survey routes and observation times were recorded using GPS-based tracking applications on mobile devices (e.g., Nike Run Club, Nike Inc Beaverton, OR, USA; Samsung Health, Samsung Electronics, Suwon-si, Gyeonggi-do, Republic of Korea) to maintain consistency in spatial coverage and survey effort across visits.Observers with prior field survey experience were preferentially recruited to ensure data reliability. All observers underwent standardized training, including case-based exercises for individual identification. When identification was uncertain, decisions were made through joint review by experienced investigators, based on predefined identification criteria and contextual information (e.g., location, group association, and repeated observations), rather than the judgment of a single observer.For each observed individual, the following variables were recorded: age class (adult or kitten), neutering status (based on ear-tipping), morphological characteristics (e.g., coat color, pattern, body shape, facial features, scars), and photographic records. Definitions and classification criteria are included in Table 1. Representative field recording sheets and photographic examples of individual identification are provided in the Supplementary material (Supplementary Figures 1, 2).Table 1Summary of variables recorded during field surveys and their definitions.VariableDefinitionSurvey roundSequential visit number within a survey year (≥5 visits per site)Age classAdult or kitten (including juveniles), determined based on morphological characteristicsNeutering statusDetermined by the presence of ear-tipping on the left earMorphological featuresCoat color, pattern, tail shape, facial structure, scars, and other distinguishing characteristicsPhoto recordsDigital images of individuals with associated GPS coordinates for identification and verificationTo support manual individual identification, a standardized recording chart (Supplementary Figure 1) developed by the research team was used, incorporating natural morphological features such as coat color, pattern distribution, eye color, tail morphology, facial structure, and other distinguishing characteristics. Individual identification was based on manual, non-invasive comparison of morphological characteristics and photographic records. This approach is relevant to feral cat monitoring, although previous work has shown that observer experience and image quality can influence individual identification from cat images (29). To improve consistency and minimize misidentification, decisions were made based on a combination of multiple features rather than a single characteristic. Ambiguous cases were resolved through consensus review among trained observers and experienced investigators.To quantify and account for imperfect detection during this observational process, within-year binary encounter histories were constructed from repeated survey visits (at least five visits per year) for each individually identifiable cat. Because individuals with all-zero encounter histories could not appear in the dataset, the single-visit detection probability (p) was estimated using a likelihood conditional on at least one detection. For standardized comparison, the cumulative probability of at least one detection over five visits was calculated as 1–(1–p)∧5. Site-year estimates were treated as supplementary because several cells had small sample sizes.For longitudinal re-identification, ear-tip status was not used as the primary matching criterion. Individuals were first matched using morphology-based features, including coat color, pattern distribution, facial markings, tail morphology, body shape, scars, and other distinctive characteristics. Ear-tip status was recorded as an indicator of neutering status, but it was not considered sufficient on its own to confirm individual identity. This was particularly important because some individuals that were not ear-tipped in an earlier survey were re-identified as ear-tipped in a later survey after undergoing TNR between survey periods. Individuals with insufficiently distinctive morphology, such as uniformly colored cats without reliable additional features, were excluded from apparent retention analyses or treated as uncertain cases. Due to uncertainty arising from factors such as rapid movement, distant observation, or uniform coat color, individual identification was not always certain. To account for this, both minimum and maximum counts were estimated. The minimum count assumed that uncertain individuals were previously observed individuals (i.e., duplicates), whereas the maximum count treated them as new individuals. The mean of these two values was defined as the mean count and used for subsequent analyses. The use of minimum and maximum counts was intended to provide a conservative estimation range that accounts for identification uncertainty in observational studies. Although this identification approach was developed specifically for this study, it was designed to ensure consistency and reproducibility through standardized criteria and observer training.2.4.Population metrics and longitudinal analysisTo evaluate population structure and dynamics, the following indicators were calculated: population abundance, expressed as counts and area-standardized density, neutering rate, kitten proportion, and individual persistence, expressed as apparent retention (i.e., the proportion of individuals observed in an earlier survey period that were re-identified in the same survey site during the subsequent survey period, reflecting observation-based persistence within the study site).Kittens were distinguished from adults based on morphological criteria, with juveniles (approximately 5–6 months old) being included in the kitten category (30). The kitten proportion was calculated as the number of kittens divided by the mean population count.Neutering status was determined based on ear-tipping, and the neutering rate was calculated as the proportion of neutered individuals relative to the mean population count.For both the descriptive status-specific comparisons and the mixed-effects analysis, neutering status was assigned according to the earlier survey of each interval (baseline status). Cats that were not ear-tipped at baseline but were re-identified as ear-tipped at the subsequent survey were retained in the baseline non-neutered category. Their later ear-tip status was recorded to document that TNR had occurred during the interval but was not used to reclassify baseline neutering status.Apparent retention was defined as the proportion of individually identifiable cats observed at an earlier survey that were re-identified at the same survey site during the subsequent survey. This observation-based metric does not distinguish continued presence from temporary absence, emigration, mortality, or failure to detect a cat that remained present. Let N(t−1) and N(t) denote the numbers of individually identifiable cats included in the re-identification dataset at the earlier and subsequent surveys, respectively, and let D denote the number observed at both surveys. The following indices were calculated:Apparent retention rate (%)=[D/N(t-1)] ×100Apparent new observation proportion (%)=[(N(t) - D)/N(t)] ×100Apparent non-retention proportion (%) =[(N(t-1) - D)/N(t-1)] ×100These indices describe changes in the observed composition of the population and should not be interpreted as direct measures of survival, mortality, immigration, emigration, or true site fidelity.2.5.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.3.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) to evaluate temporal trends, structural shifts, and habitat-specific differences while accounting for repeated observations across fixed survey sites.For count outcomes, including adult free-roaming cat counts (rounded mean counts) and total kitten counts per site, generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were applied. Although a Poisson distribution (log link) was initially considered, negative binomial models were ultimately used for final inference because they demonstrated superior model fit when evaluated using information criteria and simulation-based residual diagnostics. To evaluate overall temporal trends, survey year was treated as a continuous variable, and land-use type was included as a fixed effect. Survey site was specified as a random effect in all models to control for large between-site variations and potential sampling noise. Effects for count data are reported as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (Cis). To evaluate whether the rate of population change differed by habitat type, an interaction term between the continuous year variable and land-use type was incorporated into the population model.For the analysis of annual proportions, specifically neutering status, a binomial GLMM (logit link) was fitted to model successes vs. failures. In this model, survey year was treated as a categorical factor to estimate year-specific parameters, with land-use type included as a fixed effect and survey site as a random effect.Apparent retention…

full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Overall temporal trends in free-roaming cat populationThe combined survey area was approximately 1.49 km2 in 2017 and 2019 and 1.53 km2 from 2021 to 2025, reflecting minor boundary adjustments at two sites. Across the 17 fixed survey sites, the descriptive total mean count of free-roaming cats declined from 334.0 in 2017 to 261.0 in 2025, corresponding to an overall observed decrease of 21.9%. When expressed as a descriptive annualized metric over the 8-year interval, this represented an approximate decline of 3.0% per year. The corresponding area-standardized density declined from 223.5 to 170.9 cats/km2 (Supplementary Table 2).To formally evaluate these temporal changes while accounting for repeated observations across sites, GLMMs were fitted for the primary standardized dataset from 2017 to 2025 (Table 2). For adult free-roaming cat counts, the negative binomial GLMM provided a substantially better fit than the Poisson model based on information criteria. The model estimated a modest downward annual association in adult cat counts, corresponding to an incidence rate ratio (IRR) of 0.9676 per year (95% CI: 0.9343–1.0021; p = 0.0656). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study evaluated long-term changes in free-roaming cat populations and their structural characteristics through repeated surveys conducted at 17 sites in Seoul from 2017 to 2025. The generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) analyses support a nuanced interpretation of these long-term monitoring results. Although the descriptive total mean number of cats and population density showed a decreasing pattern over time, the formal model for adult cat counts indicated only a downward estimate that did not reach statistical significance. In contrast, the most robust population-structure changes observed during the study period were a significant decline in kitten counts and a substantial increase in model-predicted neutering probability after 2021. Until 2023, the observed neutering rate increased while the kitten proportion declined. However, this inverse year-level pattern was based on only five aggregated survey-year observations and was treated as descriptive. The site-level mixed-effects analyses showed a significant temporal decline in kitten counts and a substantial increase in neutering probability after 2021. These concurrent trends were consistent with changes in population structure but should not be interpreted as evidence that TNR alone caused the observed changes.These temporal patterns should be interpreted within the broader human and resource context of Seoul, rather than as the isolated effect of TNR alone. Factors such as intentional feeding, food-waste access, shelter availability, abandonment, caregiver activity, shelter intake and adoption practices, and community responses may also have influenced local population dynamics. Because standardized site-level data on these factors were not available across all survey sites and years, the observed associations between neutering coverage and population-structure indicators should be interpreted as patterns observed under Seoul's real-world urban management context, not as evidence that TNR alone caused all observed population changes.A key contribution of this study is that it evaluated population management outcomes using multiple indicators rather than relying solely on changes in population size. Although the overall population size declined over time, the slight decrease in neutering rate and increase in kitten proportion observed in 2025 relative to 2023 indicate that population size alone is insufficient to characterize management stability. Internal population structure and turnover dynamics must also be considered. Even with similar population sizes, some selected sites showed high neutering rates, low kitten proportions, and relatively high apparent retention, whereas others showed declining neutering rates, increased kitten proportions, and higher proportions of newly observed individuals. Available contextual information suggested that the timing and spatial distribution of TNR may have differed among these sites; however, these factors were not collected systematically and cannot be identified as causes of the observed patterns. Given that TNR implementation in Seoul is largely complaint-driven, the findings support continued monitoring and coordinated follow-up across adjacent areas rather than demonstrating that any particular intervention schedule produced the observed site-level differences.This study also demonstrates that repeated surveys within a limited spatial extent can improve the reliability and interpretability of population monitoring. Similar longitudinal monitoring principles have been applied to free-roaming animal management elsewhere. Repeated standardized route counts have been used to track street-dog population changes in Jaipur, India (31), while recent Australian cat management research similarly incorporated repeated standardized street counts to evaluate changes in free-roaming cat density (17). This type of repeated standardized monitoring is particularly useful in urban settings, where free-roaming cat populations are difficult to comprehensively census because individuals may be hidden or temporarily unobserved. In this study, each site was surveyed at least five times, and individual cats were identified using photographic records and morphological characteristics. In addition, minimum, maximum, and mean counts were estimated to account for uncertainty in individual identification. As demonstrated by the detection analysis, repeated within-year surveys reduced, but did not eliminate, uncertainty arising from imperfect detection. The pooled conditional single-visit detection probability was 0.299, corresponding to a standardized five-visit cumulative detection probability of approximately 83.1%. Year-specific cumulative detection probabilities ranged from approximately 78.1%−87.8%, indicating that approximately 12.2% to 21.9% of cats present under the model assumptions could remain undetected across five visits.These detection estimates should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. The analysis assumed constant detection probability within each pooled or year-specific model; visit-specific differences in survey effort could not be modeled explicitly, and demographic closure during each within-year survey period could not be independently verified. Survey timing may also have influenced detection, because surveys were conducted before sunset and may therefore have underdetected individuals with predominantly nocturnal or wide-ranging activity patterns. Together, these findings support use of the term apparent retention: some cats classified as not retained may have remained within the survey site but were not observed. Accordingly, apparent retention should be interpreted as observation-based persistence under standardized survey conditions, rather than as direct evidence of true site fidelity, survival, or movement behavior. These estimates quantify detection uncertainty but do not constitute formal capture–recapture estimates of abundance, and the overall results should be interpreted as reflecting relative changes and trends in population dynamics rather than absolute population estimates.Although the inverse year-level pattern between neutering rate and kitten proportion is biologically consistent with reproductive suppression following TNR, it should be interpreted cautiously. This relationship was based on only five aggregated survey-year observations, and both variables were calculated using the mean count as the denominator. Because these indicators are compositional proportions within the same observed population, part of the inverse relationship may reflect the mathematical structure of the data rather than an entirely independent demographic process. Therefore, this year-level pattern was treated as descriptive and was not interpreted as causal evidence by itself. Instead, it should be considered alongside other structural indicators, including changes in population density, apparent retention, and the proportion of newly observed individuals. The apparent retention rate, derived from repeated identification of individuals across survey periods, represents an observation-based indicator of population persistence. Neutered cats were more frequently re-identified than non-neutered cats across all intervals. One possible biological explanation for this pattern is that neutering may reduce reproductive and agonistic behaviors in free-roaming cats, which could contribute to repeated observation within the same area (32).At the same time, baseline neutering status may also reflect pre-existing differences among cats. In a complaint-driven TNR system, established or caregiver-associated cats may be more likely to have been neutered before the baseline survey and may also be more likely to be re-observed at the same site. Therefore, the association between baseline neutering status and apparent retention may partly reflect such selection and should not be interpreted as a causal effect of neutering.This interpretation should be made…
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionUrban environments are increasingly affected by the presence of free-roaming cats (Felis catus), which are a source of persistent challenges such as noise, sanitation concerns, and community conflicts. Consequently, many countries have implemented policy interventions aimed at controlling free-roaming cat populations. Within this context, management strategies for free-roaming cats have shifted from reactive approaches focused on removal or complaint-driven actions toward structured population management based on neutering and long-term monitoring (1).The Trap–Neuter–Return (TNR) approach has emerged as a central strategy in this transition. TNR involves the capture, surgical sterilization, and subsequent return of free-roaming cats to their original habitat, with the goal of suppressing reproduction and stabilizing population dynamics, ultimately reducing population size over time. However, recent studies have shown that the effectiveness of TNR is not determined solely by the number of surgeries performed, but is in fact strongly influenced by factors such as intervention intensity, spatial contiguity, and targeted implementation (1). High-intensity neutering applied across contiguous areas can result in measurable population declines, while targeted TNR in high-density or high-priority areas may contribute to improved management outcomes, such as reductions in shelter intake or kitten recruitment, when high local neutering coverage is maintained as an implementation requirement (2, 3). In high-conflict settings requiring immediate mitigation, however, TNR should not be regarded as a sufficient standalone response because its population-level effects occur gradually.At the same time, TNR should be understood as one component of a broader population-management continuum rather than as a standalone intervention. Adoption provides the most direct reduction in population size for socialized or potentially socializable cats, whereas sterilization and return-based approaches may be appropriate for healthy free-roaming cats that are unlikely to benefit from long-term sheltering or adoption. Shelter-based return-to-field programs can reduce shelter intake pressure and avoid the euthanasia of otherwise healthy cats when sheltering does not provide a realistic pathway to adoption (4–7). In addition, low-cost or free sterilization and preventive veterinary services for owned or semi-owned cats may reduce future recruitment into free-roaming populations (8–12). Therefore, effective population management requires a combination of reproductive suppression, adoption where feasible, shelter-based decision-making, caregiver engagement, public education, and management of anthropogenic food resources. More broadly, because urban free-roaming cat populations are embedded in human-dominated resource systems, management outcomes may also be influenced by food-waste access, caregiver activity, abandonment, and other local socio-environmental factors (1).One of the critical considerations in evaluating TNR effectiveness is that changes in population size alone are insufficient to fully explain population dynamics. Free-roaming cat populations are influenced by external factors such as immigration, abandonment, and compensatory reproduction driven by increased resource availability. Relying solely on population reduction as an indicator of success may therefore lead to misleading conclusions (1, 13). Recent studies have emphasized the need to incorporate multiple demographic indicators, including population abundance expressed as counts or density, neutering rate, kitten proportion, and observation-based persistence, to better understand population-level changes. However, outcomes of TNR remain context-dependent. Some studies have reported limited or inconsistent population-level effects, particularly when neutering intensity is insufficient, spatial coverage is incomplete, or immigration from surrounding areas continues (1, 13, 14). In contrast, more recent field programs have reported reductions in free-roaming cat populations, shelter intake, euthanasia, or complaints when sterilization was implemented intensively and sustained over time (2, 4–7, 15–17). These findings suggest that population-level outcomes depend strongly on local sterilization coverage, spatial targeting, intervention duration, and complementary management measures (1, 13–17). In addition, wildlife conservation perspectives have raised concerns regarding the ecological impacts of free-roaming cats, including predation on native species and broader ecosystem effects (18).These contrasting findings highlight that TNR outcomes are context-dependent and influenced by implementation strategies, ecological conditions, and study design. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation framework incorporating multiple demographic and structural indicators is essential for accurately assessing TNR effectiveness.Among these indicators, the proportion of kittens reflects reproductive activity within the population, while the neutering rate indicates the degree of reproductive suppression. Furthermore, repeated identification of individuals across survey periods provides insight into population stability and the extent of external influx. Integrating these indicators is essential for understanding how TNR policies influence population structure and dynamics.Various survey and analytical methods have been proposed to quantify free-roaming cat populations. Approaches such as line transect surveys and camera trapping, combined with statistical frameworks like spatially explicit capture–recapture, are commonly used to estimate population density while accounting for non-comprehensive detection (19–22). These methods are considered theoretically robust, as they facilitate correction for undetected individuals.However, in high-density urban environments, such as Seoul, the application of these methods faces practical limitations. The effectiveness of camera trapping is constrained by privacy concerns and limited installation sites, while complex urban structures can reduce detection efficiency due to restricted visibility. Similarly, line transect surveys require consistent observation along predefined routes, which can be difficult to maintain in cities with irregular road networks and limited accessibility.To address these constraints, this study employed a field-based survey approach designed to maximize the number of individuals observed within a defined area and time frame. By repeatedly surveying fixed locations, this approach enables the analysis of relative changes in population size and density over time, as well as population structure. Rather than estimating absolute population size, this study instead focuses on temporal trends and population dynamics derived from repeated observations.Changes in free-roaming cat populations do not occur over short time scales, but are influenced by cumulative temporal and spatial factors. Longitudinal data based on repeated surveys of the same locations are therefore essential for evaluating the real-world effectiveness of TNR policies.Seoul provides a valuable urban case for such analysis. Since 2008, the Seoul Metropolitan Government has implemented a publicly funded TNR program with increasing annual procedure numbers. According to official reports, the annual number of TNR procedures increased from approximately 5,800 in 2010 to over 10,000 after 2018, reaching approximately 14,000 by 2025, demonstrating the scale of municipal program input rather than, by itself, evidence of control efficacy or intensified population impact (23, 24). These city-wide procedure counts indicate the scale of program input, but they do not directly represent neutering coverage within specific territorial units. Indeed, increasing procedure numbers may also reflect persistent management demand due to remaining unneutered cats, ongoing reproduction, abandonment, immigration from surro…

papers.title_original: Beyond population size: long-term changes in free-roaming cat population structure during TNR implementation in Seoul

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand long-term changes in free-roaming cat population structure during the implementation of a TNR program in Seoul, focusing on how neutering rates and kitten proportions affect population dynamics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A longitudinal study was conducted in Seoul from 2017 onward, involving 17 sites selected based on land-use classifications. Sites with densities approximating the citywide average were preferentially chosen to avoid overrepresentation of extreme conditions.
analysis.methods: Population size, neutering rate, kitten proportion, and apparent retention were calculated using non-invasive photographic individual identification. A logistic mixed effects model assessed apparent retention by baseline neutering status, and within-year encounter histories were used to estimate detection probability.
analysis.main_results: Overall population size and density showed a decreasing temporal pattern, while neutering rates generally increased and kitten proportions generally decreased. Cats neutered at baseline had significantly higher odds of apparent retention than non-neutered cats (OR = 3.06, 95% CI: 2.07–4.53).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings describe population-structure patterns observed during the implementation of Seoul's public TNR program, including reduced kitten counts and increased neutering probability over time.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results inform the understanding of how TNR programs can influence feral cat population dynamics, offering insights into the effectiveness of neutering in reducing kitten proportions and increasing apparent retention.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Site-year estimates were treated as supplementary due to small sample sizes in several cells, and ear-tip status was not used as the primary matching criterion for longitudinal re-identification.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines long-term changes in free-roaming cat population structure during the implementation of a TNR program in Seoul. It highlights how neutering rates and kitten proportions influence population dynamics, showing a decreasing trend in population size and density, alongside increasing neutering rates and decreasing kitten proportions. The findings suggest that neutering significantly increases the odds of apparent retention, with cats neutered at baseline having 3.06 times higher odds of being re-identified compared to non-neutered cats (95% CI: 2.07–4.53). These results provide insights into the effectiveness of TNR programs in managing feral cat populations, particularly in reducing kitten counts and promoting retention. However, the study acknowledges limitations, such as the use of supplementary site-year estimates due to small sample sizes and the exclusion of ear-tip status as a primary matching criterion. The evidence is moderate in strength, as the study relies on non-invasive photographic identification and longitudinal analysis, which may introduce some uncertainty.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解首尔实施 TNR 计划期间自由流浪猫种群结构的长期变化,重点关注绝育率和小猫比例如何影响种群动态。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 从 2017 年起,首尔进行了一项纵向研究,涉及根据土地利用分类选择的 17 个地点。优先选择密度接近全市平均水平的地点,以避免过度代表极端条件。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用非侵入性摄影个体识别来计算种群规模、绝育率、小猫比例和表观保留率。逻辑混合效应模型通过基线绝育状态评估表观保留,并使用一年内的遭遇历史来估计检测概率。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果描述了首尔公共 TNR 计划实施期间观察到的种群结构模式,包括随着时间的推移,小猫数量减少和绝育概率增加。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果有助于了解 TNR 计划如何影响野猫种群动态,并深入了解绝育在减少小猫比例和增加表观保留方面的有效性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于几个单元中的样本量较小,站点年份估计被视为补充,并且耳尖状态未被用作纵向重新识别的主要匹配标准。

This is the fourteenth confirmed case of animal rabies in 2026. North Carolina law requires that all domestic pets (cats, dogs and ferrets), whether living inside or outside, aged four months or older be vaccinated for rabies. Animals that are confined in outdoor fenced areas should also have current rabies vaccinations. Supervising pets when they are outdoors could prevent contact with wild animals and lessen the possibility of rabies exposure. Guilford County Animal Services may be contacted for more information on rabies prevention at 336-641-2506 or visit our Animal Services website. For information regarding the current rabies cases, please contact Jorge Ortega at 336-641-3409 or jortega1@guilfordcountync.gov. Rabies circulates within our wildlife population throughout the entire year. Here are some tips to help prevent you or your family from being exposed to the rabies virus: Avoid direct contact with wildlife, dead or alive. Do not approach, try to play with, touch, rescue or treat any wildlife. If you find a sick or injured animal, contact Animal Control at 336-641-5990. Avoid any animal displaying unnatural behavior. Wild animals are not usually friendly so be very careful if they approach you. Do not try to separate fighting animals. Feed your pets indoors. Leaving food outside will attract dogs, cats and other wildlife into your yard. Report all stray animals to Animal Control at 336-641-5990 in Greensboro and 336-883-3224 in High Point. Stray animals may not have current rabies vaccinations. If a person is bitten by an animal (domestic or stray), wash the bitten area immediately with soap and water, seek medical attention, and report the bite to local Animal Control Officers. General Programme of Work Building a Healthier Africa, Together: A manifesto for transformation WHO Africa / Countries / Nigeria / Nigeria steps up action to prevent rabies deaths through One Health approach Nigeria steps up action to prevent rabies deaths through One Health approach 7 October 2026 | Feature Story | Reading time: 4 min Nigeria steps up action to prevent rabies deaths through One Health approach More pictures More images Abuja, Nigeria is strengthening dog vaccination, surveillance and public awareness to prevent rabies deaths and advance efforts to end human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. The 2026 World Rabies Day commemoration on 28 September brought together government institutions and partners under the theme “Stronger Together”, with a call for coordinated action across the human, animal and environmental health sectors. Rabies is fatal once clinical symptoms appear, but it is preventable. Vaccinating dogs, preventing bites and ensuring people receive prompt treatment after exposure can save lives. Rabies awareness activities are helping people understand the disease and how to prevent it. During a sensitization campaign, Daniel Mshelia, a security guard who works around dogs, learnt about the risks of rabies, the importance of dog vaccination and the need to seek care immediately after an animal bite. “Before then, I knew little about rabies or the danger an infected animal could pose. I learnt that a dog bite could lead to death if treatment is not sought early,” he recalled. His experience shows the importance of ensuring people know how to prevent rabies and what to do after possible exposure. Preventing rabies at its source At the World Rabies Day commemoration in Abuja, the Federal Government reaffirmed its commitment to ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. “Protecting communities from rabies requires everyone to play a part. We must stop working in silos and continue to educate families, encourage responsible animal ownership, and work together to reduce risks in our communities,” said Dr Chinyere Ijeoma Akujobi, Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Livestock Development. According to the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development, more than 100 animal rabies cases were recorded between January and August 2026 across 16 states. Nigeria is strengthening rabies prevention through a One Health approach that brings together the human, animal and environmental health sectors, as the country works towards the global goal of ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. The Federal Ministry of Livestock Development leads animal surveillance, dog vaccination and veterinary services. The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare supports surveillance of human exposures and access to care, while the Federal Ministry of Environment supports public awareness and safer interaction between people and animals. Mrs Dorcas Mernyi, Assistant Director, Rabies Programme Manager and One Health Desk Officer at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, called for prompt care following exposure. “No one should die from rabies simply because they did not know what to do after a dog bite or could not access treatment. We must ensure health workers recognise possible exposure immediately and that patients receive appropriate care without delay. Strengthening surveillance and response In November 2025, the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO) and other One Health partners, convened a national workshop to review, test and validate the Rabies Rapid Response Toolkit. The toolkit guides surveillance, investigation and response to suspected rabies events. It helps teams identify people who may have been exposed, improve reporting and coordinate action between public health and veterinary services. WHO also supports government-led rabies investigations through technical guidance on surveillance, risk assessment and response coordination. Dr Alexander Chimbaru, WHO Emergency Preparedness and Response Cluster Lead in Nigeria, said preventing deaths requires action throughout the year. “Ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies requires sustained collaboration between government, health and veterinary professionals, communities and dog owners. Every dog vaccinated, every exposure reported early and every person who receives timely care takes us closer to the 2030 goal.” Acting quickly can save lives The NCDC one health toolkit advises that anyone bitten or scratched by an animal suspected of having rabies should immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical care without delay. Depending on the exposure, PEP may include rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin or monoclonal antibodies. People should not wait for symptoms before seeking care. Preventing infection in dogs is equally important. WHO recommends sustained vaccination coverage of at least 70% of dogs in at-risk areas to interrupt transmission. WHO will continue to support the Government of Nigeria and partners to strengthen rabies prevention, surveillance and response towards ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. news.content: FOX8 WGHP Guilford County confirms 14th case of animal rabies in 2026 Jim Sands 2 days ago GUILFORD COUNTY, N.C. (WGHP) — The Guilford County Health and Human Services Agency, Department of Public Health, is alerting residents that another case of animal rabies has been reported. The agency discovered a raccoon on Kearn Street in Jamestown that tested positive for the rabies virus on Thursday. This is the 14th confirmed case of animal rabies in 2026. Rabies circulates within the local wildlife population throughout the year. Top headlines on MyFOX8.com Piedmont Triad emergency personnel are in position to assist with Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias relief in western North Carolina Winston-Salem man charged with rape of a child Greensboro Fire Department sends 17 to western North Carolina to help with Hurricane Isaias View all NC news » North Carolina law requires that all domestic pets (cats, dogs and ferrets), whether living inside or outside, aged four months or older, be vaccinated for rabies. Animals that are confined in outdoor fenced areas should also have current rabies vaccinations. Supervising pets when they are outdoors could prevent contact with wild animals and lessen the possibility of rabies exposure. Guilford County Animal Services may be contacted for more information on rabies prevention at 336-641-2506 or visit www.guilfordcountync.gov/animalservices. For information regarding the current rabies case, contact Jorge Ortega at 336-641-3409 or jortega1@guilfordcountync.gov. Tips to help prevent you or your family from being exposed to rabies Avoid direct contact with wildlife, dead or alive. Do not approach, try to play with, touch, rescue or treat any wildlife. If you find a sick or injured animal, contact Animal Control at 336-641-5990. Avoid any animal displaying unnatural behavior. Wild animals are not usually friendly so be very careful if they approach you. Do not try to separate fighting animals. Feed your pets indoors. Leaving food outside will attract dogs, cats and other wildlife into your yard. Report all stray animals to Animal Control at 336-641-5990 in Greensboro and 336-883-3224 in High Point. Stray animals may not have current rabies vaccinations. If a person is bitten by an animal (domestic or stray), wash the bitten area immediately with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the bite to local animal control officers. Once the virus reaches the central nervous system and clinical symptoms appear, mortality approaches 100 percent, and the World Health Organization estimates that roughly 59,000 people die of the disease each year, with nearly half of the victims children under the age of fifteen. Although effective vaccines and rabies immunoglobulins exist, their cost and chronic global supply shortages leave many people in rural Asia and Africa dangerously unprotected after exposure to a rabid animal. A new study published in PLOS Pathogens now offers a strikingly practical way forward: researchers report that diltiazem, a cheap and widely used FDA-approved blood pressure medication, blocks the entry of rabies virus into cells and rescued approximately 70 percent of mice from a lethal infection. The research, led by Ziruo Sun, Jinliang Wang, Zhigao Bu and colleagues at the Harbin Veterinary Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, began with a systematic search for the host machinery that rabies virus depends on to invade cells. In a previous genome-wide screen, the team had used 64,755 small interfering RNAs targeting 21,585 human genes in HEK293 cells to identify host factors required for rabies virus replication. Among the hits were sixteen genes related to potassium channels, and the strongest effect came from silencing KCNMA1, the gene that encodes the pore-forming subunit of the large conductance calcium- and voltage-activated potassium channel known as KCa1.1, a seven-transmembrane protein sitting in the plasma membrane. To confirm that this channel genuinely matters for infection, the researchers knocked down KCa1.1 expression in both mouse neuroblastoma N2a cells and human HEK293 cells using specific siRNAs. Quantitative PCR verified that the channel’s mRNA was substantially reduced, and when the silenced cells were infected with a recombinant rabies virus strain expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein, the amount of infectious virus released into the culture supernatant dropped significantly at both 24 and 48 hours after infection. The team then turned to paxilline, a selective chemical inhibitor of KCa1.1 that binds the inner pore of the channel and blocks potassium conductance. In N2a, HEK293, and human SK-N-SH neuroblastoma cells, paxilline had no effect on cell viability but suppressed rabies virus replication in a clear dose-dependent manner, and time-course experiments confirmed the inhibition persisted across the tested period. Because KCa1.1 is expressed primarily at the plasma membrane, the investigators hypothesized that it might act during viral entry rather than during later stages of the viral life cycle. Entry involves two separable steps: attachment of virus particles to the cell surface and their subsequent internalization. By incubating cells with virus at 4 degrees Celsius, a temperature that permits binding but prevents internalization, and then quantifying attached viral RNA, the team showed that neither KCa1.1 silencing nor paxilline treatment changed how much virus bound to cells. When the temperature was shifted to 37 degrees to allow entry, however, and surface-bound virus was stripped away with trypsin before analysis, the amount of viral RNA inside treated or silenced cells fell dramatically. A complementary microscopy assay, which labeled viral glycoprotein under conditions that distinguish particles remaining on the surface from those that had entered, showed that paxilline-treated cells accumulated more virus on their surface while their total particle count stayed the same. Together, these experiments demonstrated that activated KCa1.1 is specifically required for the internalization step of rabies virus entry. A co-immunoprecipitation assay revealed that KCa1.1 does not physically interact with the rabies virus glycoprotein, the viral surface protein that drives attachment and clathrin-mediated endocytosis. That result pointed to an intermediary. Prior work had shown that KCa1.1 assembles into macromolecular complexes with voltage-gated calcium channels, including Cav1.2, and that calcium influx through these channels can activate KCa1.1. Notably, Cav1.2 was the only calcium channel that emerged from the team’s earlier genome-wide screen. Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed a specific interaction between Cav1.2 and KCa1.1, and silencing Cav1.2 in N2a and HEK293 cells significantly reduced rabies virus titers, establishing that the L-type calcium channel is also required for productive infection. The mechanistic picture became sharper when the researchers examined the role of the viral glycoprotein itself. Co-immunoprecipitation showed that Cav1.2 specifically interacts with the rabies virus glycoprotein, and a pull-down assay using purified virus particles demonstrated that Cav1.2 captures rabies virions in a dose-dependent manner. Binding assays revealed that Cav1.2 silencing or blockade did not reduce how much virus attached to cells, but internalization assays showed far less viral RNA inside treated cells. In other words, the glycoprotein engages Cav1.2, and this engagement is required to activate the channel and trigger the internalization machinery, even though the virus still docks normally on the cell surface when the channel is disabled. The team also identified the downstream cellular process that the channel axis manipulates. Rabies virus enters cells through clathrin-mediated endocytosis with the help of actin, and previous work had shown that KCa1.1 promotes influenza virus entry by regulating F-actin polymerization. Using phalloidin staining to visualize filamentous actin, the researchers found that rabies virus entry induces F-actin polymerization in HEK293 cells, and that this polymerization was markedly reduced when Cav1.2 or KCa1.1 were knocked down or when cells were treated with diltiazem or paxilline. The authors therefore propose a sequential model: rabies virus glycoprotein binds Cav1.2 and triggers its activation; activated Cav1.2 then interacts with and activates KCa1.1; and activated KCa1.1 drives F-actin polymerization that powers the internalization of the virus particle. The therapeutic implications rest on diltiazem, a benzothiazepine-class L-type calcium channel blocker approved in the United States in 1982 and long prescribed for hypertension, angina, and atrial arrhythmias. In cell culture, diltiazem blocked rabies virus infection in a dose-dependent manner without affecting viability, and four other FDA-approved Cav1.2 antagonists, the phenylalkylamine verapamil and the dihydropyridines nifedipine, nicardipine, and nimodipine, also inhibited the virus in vitro. The decisive test came in mice. Six-week-old C57BL/6J mice were inoculated intramuscularly with ten 50 percent mouse lethal doses of the rabies street virus GX/09, and six hours later they began receiving daily intramuscular injections of diltiazem at 25 or 50 milligrams per kilogram, or a phosphate buffer control. All 19 control mice died within 9 to 16 days with typical rabies signs such as body tremors and hind limb paralysis. At the lower dose, 5 of 19 mice survived, roughly 26 percent, while at 50 milligrams per kilogram, 13 of 19 mice survived, approximately 70 percent, and the survivors remained completely asymptomatic throughout a 28-day observation period. Measurements of viral burden supported the idea that diltiazem works by blocking entry before the virus reaches the brain. No viral RNA was detectable in the brains of treated or control mice at day 4, but by day 6, viral RNA was present in all six control animals examined and in only two of six diltiazem-treated animals, and immunohistochemistry at day 8 detected rabies antigen in all control brains but only one of three treated brains. When the researchers delayed diltiazem administration until days 6 and 7, after viral replication was already underway in the brain, they observed no significant reduction in brain viral RNA, indicating that the drug’s protection is unlikely to stem from direct suppression of established central nervous system infection. Notably, the 50 milligram per kilogram mouse dose corresponds, after body surface area normalization under FDA guidelines, to a human equivalent dose of roughly 4 milligrams per kilogram, or about 240 milligrams per day for a 60-kilogram adult, which falls squarely within the range already used clinically for cardiovascular indications. The authors argue that diltiazem could serve as an affordable, mass-produced complement to existing post-exposure prophylaxis, offering a stopgap where rabies immunoglobulin is unavailable and a potential enhancement where it is not, since it is estimated that only 1 to 10 percent of category III exposure patients currently receive the recommended treatment. The findings also extend a growing body of evidence that ion channels are conserved entry factors for diverse viruses: Cav1.2 has been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 and influenza virus entry, KCa1.1 in influenza virus endocytosis, and diltiazem has shown activity against rotavirus, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus, and porcine deltacoronavirus. With no approved drugs currently targeting KCa1.1, the potassium channel remains a target for future drug development, while Cav1.2, already served by three structural classes of clinically validated antagonists, stands out as a promising foundation for broad-spectrum antiviral strategies. Further studies will be needed to evaluate the in vivo efficacy of the other calcium channel blockers and to determine whether diltiazem concentrations in the central nervous system reach antiviral levels, but the prospect of repurposing a decades-old cardiovascular pill against one of humanity’s most lethal pathogens gives the global effort to eliminate rabies deaths a genuinely new weapon to test. analysis.brief_en: A study published on October 10, 2026, in PLOS Pathogens reveals that diltiazem, a common blood pressure medication, can block the entry of rabies virus into cells and save infected mice. The study highlights the potential of repurposing existing drugs for rabies treatment, offering hope for improving global access to care.

Summary Penang has not reported any human rabies cases since 1975, nor any animal cases to date, as stated by State Youth, Sports, and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen. The Penang State Health Department and the Department of Veterinary Services continue to monitor the situation and remain prepared to respond to potential incidents. First Published: Monday, 05 Oct 2026 5:17 PM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter Subscribe GEORGE TOWN, Oct 5 — Penang has recorded no human rabies cases since the last two cases were reported in 1975, with the Penang State Health Department remaining on standby to respond to any possible cases. State Youth, Sports and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen said no animal rabies cases had also been detected in the state to date. “No new cases have been reported thus far, but we are always prepared to deal with any incidents,” he said at a press conference for the Penang state-level Clean, Smoke-Free Premises Programme at Food Bayana Medan here today. Gooi said the state government was also working with the Department of Veterinary Services to monitor the rabies situation in Penang. He advised the public to follow Ministry of Health guidelines if bitten by an animal, including seeking immediate medical attention at any healthcare facility to ensure those exposed to infection risks receive proper examination and appropriate treatment. On Sept 27, a 31-year-old man from Kubang Pasu, Kedah, died of rabies after reportedly being bitten by a stray dog in August, marking the first human rabies case reported in the state since 1998. — Bernama You May Also Like Related Articles Malaysia / 6 m ago Malaysia has spent decades digitising public healthcare. Summary Penang has not reported any human rabies cases since 1975, nor any animal cases to date, as stated by State Youth, Sports, and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen. The Penang State Health Department and the Department of Veterinary Services continue to monitor the situation and remain prepared to respond to potential incidents. First Published: Monday, 05 Oct 2026 5:17 PM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter Subscribe GEORGE TOWN, Oct 5 — Penang has recorded no human rabies cases since the last two cases were reported in 1975, with the Penang State Health Department remaining on standby to respond to any possible cases. State Youth, Sports and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen said no animal rabies cases had also been detected in the state to date. “No new cases have been reported thus far, but we are always prepared to deal with any incidents,” he said at a press conference for the Penang state-level Clean, Smoke-Free Premises Programme at Food Bayana Medan here today. Gooi said the state government was also working with the Department of Veterinary Services to monitor the rabies situation in Penang. He advised the public to follow Ministry of Health guidelines if bitten by an animal, including seeking immediate medical attention at any healthcare facility to ensure those exposed to infection risks receive proper examination and appropriate treatment. On Sept 27, a 31-year-old man from Kubang Pasu, Kedah, died of rabies after reportedly being bitten by a stray dog in August, marking the first human rabies case reported in the state since 1998. — Bernama You May Also Like Related Articles Malaysia / 6 m ago Malaysia has spent decades digitising public healthcare. news.source_body_en: Penang, Malaysia, has remained on alert for human rabies following the death of a 31-year-old man from Kedah on September 27, 2026, who succumbed to the infection after being bitten by a stray dog in August. This marks the first human rabies case in Kedah since 1998. Penang has not reported any human rabies cases since 1975, and no animal rabies cases have been detected in the state. State Health Department officials, including Daniel Gooi Zi Sen, have confirmed the absence of new cases but emphasized preparedness for potential incidents. They are collaborating with the Department of Veterinary Services to monitor the situation and advise the public to follow Ministry of Health guidelines for animal bites, such as seeking immediate medical attention. The response is ongoing, with authorities maintaining vigilance and ensuring adherence to protocols to prevent further spread.
news.content_zh: 2026 年 9 月 27 日,一名来自吉打州的 31 岁男子在 8 月份被流浪狗咬伤后死于感染,马来西亚槟城一直对人类 狂犬病 保持警惕。这是吉打州自 1998 年以来首例人类 狂犬病 病例。槟城自 1975 年以来就没有报告过任何人类 狂犬病 病例,该州也没有发现任何动物 狂犬病 病例。包括丹尼尔·古伊·兹森在内的州卫生部门官员已证实没有新病例,但强调为潜在事件做好准备。他们正在与兽医服务部合作监测情况,并建议公众遵循卫生部关于动物咬伤的指导方针,例如立即就医。应对措施仍在继续,当局保持警惕并确保遵守协议以防止进一步传播。

Why is the ORV program conducted in Appalachians? topics: Rabies USDA Oral rabies vaccination Wildlife Services North Carolina Asheville Helicopter baiting Raccoons WESTERN NORTH CAROLINA (WLOS) — Oral Rabies Vaccination (ORV) bait drops are planned for this week in the mountains of western North Carolina. According to a news release from the United States Department of Agriculture, the drops will be made in the area on the following days: Oct. 5-9: Ground teams will distribute baits by vehicle in the Asheville city limits. Oct. 9-13: Helicopter baiting will be conducted in the urban and suburban communities in greater Asheville, Burnsville, Mars Hill and Waynesville Oct. 15-22: Low-flying airplanes will be dropping baits in the rural areas of the following counties: Ashe, Avery, Buncombe, Cherokee, Clay, Graham, Haywood, Henderson, Jackson, Macon, Madison, McDowell, Mitchell, Swain, Transylvania, Watauga, and Yancey The USDA said it is conducting this drops in coordination with Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Wildlife Services and the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services. The USDA said in the release that the smell of the ORV baits attracts targeted wild animals, such as raccoons, who eat the baits and are then vaccinated against rabies. HELENE DEBRIS 'STILL A FACTOR' IN NC WILDFIRE RISK, OFFICIAL SAYS Powered By 10 Sec Pensacola home catches fire before Isaias nears peak; officer rescues trapped man Next Stay The ORV bait distribution program is part of management activities to prevent the westward movement of the rabies virus most often spread by raccoons, the release said. ORV baits are distributed using small airplanes and helicopters from the air and vehicles on the ground. The project is based out of multiple airport locations and will take place for about three weeks in October. During the baiting program more than 2.4 million baits will be distributed in areas of western North Carolina, southwest Virginia, east Tennessee, northcentral Alabama and north Georgia, including over 600,000 baits in North Carolina, the release said. All baiting efforts should be completed by late October, depending on weather and other factors. Rabies is caused by a virus that infects the central nervous system in mammals and represents a serious public health concern. If exposures to the virus are not treated it is almost always fatal, the USDA said. Costs associated with detection, prevention and control of rabies exceed $600 million annually in the U.S. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 90 percent of reported rabies cases in the U.S. are in wildlife. CAMP LIKE IT’S THE 1900S: CRADLE OF FORESTRY HOSTS OLD-STYLE CAMPING EVENT People are urged not to make contact with or feed wildlife and to keep their pets’ rabies vaccinations current. The USDA said in the release that the vaccine baits have been proven safe in many species of animals, including domestic dogs and cats. Humans and pets cannot get rabies from contact with the baits but are asked to leave them undisturbed should they encounter them. If contact with baits occurs, immediately rinse the contact area with warm water and soap. According to the release, ORV baits have been distributed in North Carolina since 2005 as part of a larger effort by the Wildlife Services, National Rabies Management Program to prevent the westward spread of raccoon rabies by creating a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains from the Canadian border to Alabama. news.content_zh: The USDA is planning rabies vaccine bait drops in western North Carolina this week as part of an Oral Rabies Vaccination (ORV) program to prevent the westward spread of the rabies virus. The program will involve ground teams distributing baits from October 5-9 in Asheville city limits, helicopter baiting in urban and suburban areas from October 9-13, and low-flying airplanes dropping baits in rural counties from October 15-22. Over 2.4 million baits will be distributed across western North Carolina, southwest Virginia, east Tennessee, northcentral Alabama, and north Georgia, with more than 600,000 in North Carolina alone. The ORV program aims to create a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains to stop the spread of raccoon rabies. The USDA emphasized that rabies is a serious public health concern, and untreated exposures are almost always fatal. The baiting efforts are expected to be completed by late October, depending on weather and other factors. The program is conducted in coordination with the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Wildlife Services, and the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services. The vaccine baits are safe for many species, including domestic dogs and cats, and humans and pets are advised not to make contact with or feed wildlife and to keep their pets’ rabies vaccinations current.

Public Media Careers Internships Volunteer Ways to Donate Sponsor Our Programs Newsletters Search Health Bat-human interactions are on the rise, leading to rabies concerns Ideastream Public Media | By Ida Lieszkovszky Published October 5, 2026 at 5:45 AM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 1:00 Ivan Kuzmin / Adobe Stock Images Experts recommend calling your local health department if you have been exposed to bats, such as these big brown bats that have moved into an attic. There has been an uptick in the number of bats testing positive for rabies both locally and nationwide, though experts caution that doesn’t mean rabies rates are on the rise. So far this year, five bats have tested positive for rabies in Cuyahoga County, double the normal amount. “That was unusual because typically in Cuyahoga County, we see maybe one or two positive bats for an entire year,” said Stacey Koltas, an environmental health program manager at the Cuyahoga County Board of Health. A total of 107 bats have been sent for testing so far this year from Cuyahoga County, compared with about 50 in a typical year. Koltas said that shows the number of bat-human interactions are up, because those interactions are what trigger testing. “When you increase the denominator like that, you dilute the rate, and so what we're seeing still is an infectivity rate that's within what we expect to see, both at the county level and at the state level,” Koltas said. The reason for the rise in human encounters with bats isn't yet fully understood, she said. State and federal tracking has seen the same trend. “We’ve already tested more animals this year than we usually do for an entire 12-month period," Ohio State Public Health Veterinarian Sara Margrey said in an emailed statement. The increase includes a 143% increase in bat submissions compared to 2022-2025, Margrey said, though the positivity rate is still within the normal range of about 3.6% of bats tested. The Centers for Disease Control sent out an advisory last month warning of a “nationwide increase in reported human rabies exposures.” There has not been a human case of rabies in Ohio since 1970 — largely because of treatment (including the rabies vaccine) given to people who've been exposed to rabid animals. In the U.S. overall, about 100,000 people each year receive that treatment after encountering rabid animals. If you do come into contact with a bat, or wake to find one in your home, Koltas recommended calling your local health department to be evaluated. “We can either send the bat to our state lab for rabies testing, to rule out the risk for rabies, or advise the individuals who were exposed to receive the post-exposure prophylaxis,” she said. Why encounters are on the rise While the reason for the uptick in bat-human interactions is unknown, Koltas speculated that it could be because bat populations are finally starting to rebound, after having been decimated by disease over the past several years. According to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, bat numbers are stabilizing in some species but not necessarily increasing. University of Cincinnati Associate Professor Joseph Johnson, the principal investigator of The Ohio Bat Lab, said in an e-mail that “bat populations are hard to quantify.” He also noted that it’s difficult to track rabies levels in bats because they need to be killed, or already dead, for their brains to be tested for the disease. They are also a protected species, making random testing impossible. “This means... the tests we get come from encounters with sick animals, which is a little bit of a sampling bias and needs to be interpreted with a grain of salt,” he said. Johnson noted that it’s never a good idea to touch or pick up wildlife. It’s not just bats that can spread rabies. In Ohio, raccoons, skunks, coyotes and foxes can also spread the disease and pets are also capable of being infected. But humans tend to have more interactions with bats than with other species because bats tend to take refuge in warm places such as houses when winter is on the horizon. Public Media Careers Internships Volunteer Ways to Donate Sponsor Our Programs Newsletters Search Health Bat-human interactions are on the rise, leading to rabies concerns Ideastream Public Media | By Ida Lieszkovszky Published October 5, 2026 at 5:45 AM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 1:00 Ivan Kuzmin / Adobe Stock Images Experts recommend calling your local health department if you have been exposed to bats, such as these big brown bats that have moved into an attic. There has been an uptick in the number of bats testing positive for rabies both locally and nationwide, though experts caution that doesn’t mean rabies rates are on the rise. So far this year, five bats have tested positive for rabies in Cuyahoga County, double the normal amount. “That was unusual because typically in Cuyahoga County, we see maybe one or two positive bats for an entire year,” said Stacey Koltas, an environmental health program manager at the Cuyahoga County Board of Health. A total of 107 bats have been sent for testing so far this year from Cuyahoga County, compared with about 50 in a typical year. Koltas said that shows the number of bat-human interactions are up, because those interactions are what trigger testing. “When you increase the denominator like that, you dilute the rate, and so what we're seeing still is an infectivity rate that's within what we expect to see, both at the county level and at the state level,” Koltas said. The reason for the rise in human encounters with bats isn't yet fully understood, she said. State and federal tracking has seen the same trend. “We’ve already tested more animals this year than we usually do for an entire 12-month period," Ohio State Public Health Veterinarian Sara Margrey said in an emailed statement. The increase includes a 143% increase in bat submissions compared to 2022-2025, Margrey said, though the positivity rate is still within the normal range of about 3.6% of bats tested. The Centers for Disease Control sent out an advisory last month warning of a “nationwide increase in reported human rabies exposures.” There has not been a human case of rabies in Ohio since 1970 — largely because of treatment (including the rabies vaccine) given to people who've been exposed to rabid animals. In the U.S. overall, about 100,000 people each year receive that treatment after encountering rabid animals. If you do come into contact with a bat, or wake to find one in your home, Koltas recommended calling your local health department to be evaluated. “We can either send the bat to our state lab for rabies testing, to rule out the risk for rabies, or advise the individuals who were exposed to receive the post-exposure prophylaxis,” she said. Why encounters are on the rise While the reason for the uptick in bat-human interactions is unknown, Koltas speculated that it could be because bat populations are finally starting to rebound, after having been decimated by disease over the past several years. According to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, bat numbers are stabilizing in some species but not necessarily increasing. University of Cincinnati Associate Professor Joseph Johnson, the principal investigator of The Ohio Bat Lab, said in an e-mail that “bat populations are hard to quantify.” He also noted that it’s difficult to track rabies levels in bats because they need to be killed, or already dead, for their brains to be tested for the disease. They are also a protected species, making random testing impossible. “This means... the tests we get come from encounters with sick animals, which is a little bit of a sampling bias and needs to be interpreted with a grain of salt,” he said. Johnson noted that it’s never a good idea to touch or pick up wildlife. It’s not just bats that can spread rabies. In Ohio, raccoons, skunks, coyotes and foxes can also spread the disease and pets are also capable of being infected. But humans tend to have more interactions with bats than with other species because bats tend to take refuge in warm places such as houses when winter is on the horizon. news.content_zh: 该文章报告称,俄亥俄州凯霍加县蝙蝠与人类的互动有所增加,导致进行了更多的 狂犬病 测试。今年,有 5 只蝙蝠的 狂犬病 检测呈阳性,数量是平时的两倍,到目前为止,总共有 107 只蝙蝠接受了检测,而通常年份约为 50 只。阳性率保持在3.6%的正常范围内。专家推测,相互作用的增加可能是由于蝙蝠种群在过去的疾病影响后恢复,尽管这一点尚未得到证实。CDC 注意到全国范围内报告的人类 狂犬病 暴露量有所增加,但自 1970 年以来,俄亥俄州没有记录到人类病例,这主要归功于有效的 暴露后预防 治疗。当局建议如果接触蝙蝠,请联系当地卫生部门,以评估风险并接受适当的医疗护理。
