news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Isaias World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Atlanta | News Weather Meet Our Team News Tips 65° Contact Us Download with Damez Download Our App Advertise Memorials Watch CBS News Local News USDA to airdrop rabies vaccine baits across Northwest Georgia in effort to stop virus's spread By Dan Raby Dan Raby Senior Digital Producer, CBS News Atlanta Dan Raby, the senior digital producer for CBS News Atlanta, has been covering everything happening around Georgia for more than a decade. Read Full Bio Dan Raby October 7, 2026 / 2:58 PM EDT / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google The federal government is planning to airdrop more than 500,000 tiny packages that smell like fish across northwest Georgia in the next few weeks in an ongoing effort to protect the state's residents. The massive aerial operation is part of an annual operation to spread rabies vaccination baits targeting raccoons and other wildlife in the state. According to the USDA, more than 500,000 baits containing the RABORAL V-RG® oral rabies vaccine (ORV) will be spread across over 7,000 square kilometers in parts of Bartow, Catoosa, Chattooga, Dade, Floyd, Fannin, Gilmer, Gordon, Murray, Pickens, Rabun, Towns, Union, Walker, and Whitfield counties. The goal of the multi-state operation is to stop the spread of rabies westward and, along with other operations by the USDA, eventually eliminate terrestrial rabies from the United States. When will the rabies vaccine be airdropped? The Walker County government said that helicopter bait drops will begin on or about Oct. 7. Airplane drops will start around Oct. 20. Officials say residents in the affected counties should expect to spot low-flying airplanes or helicopters during these times. The program is a cooperative effort between the USDA, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Georgia Department of Public Health, and other local and federal agencies. It aims to reduce a significant human health and safety threat associated with rabies. Officials say the public should not try to touch or move the rabies vaccination bait. USDA What are rabies bait packets? The baits, packets coated with fishmeal crumbles, are designed to attract raccoons and other wildlife. Each bait is labeled with a toll-free information number, allowing residents to report any contact or ask questions. Officials advise the public not to touch or move the baits. If a bait is found in an open area, it can be carefully tossed deeper into the woods using gloves or a paper towel. People should wash their hands immediately if they come into contact with the vaccine inside a bait and contact their local health department for guidance. While the baits are not harmful to pets, eating several may cause mild stomach upset. Christopher Harris contributed to this report. FOX 13 News Orlando News - FOX 35 Orlando Gainesville News - FOX 51 Gainesville Stream on FOX One Watch NFL Games Watch College Football Games Watch MLB Games Watch NASCAR Cup Series Watch IndyCar Series Watch Men's College Basketball Watch Women's College Basketball Watch WNBA Games Watch MLS Games High Wind Warning until SUN 8:00 AM EDT, Clay County 3 Flood Watch until SUN 2:00 PM EDT, Hart County, Habersham County, Stephens County, Elbert County, Rabun County, Franklin County Flood Watch until SUN 8:00 AM EDT, Towns County, Rockdale County, Jackson County, Banks County, Newton County, Lumpkin County, Gwinnett County, White County, Jasper County, Morgan County, Putnam County, Oconee County, Madison County, Hall County, Oglethorpe County, Barrow County, Walton County, Clarke County, Greene County, Union County Rabies vaccine baits to be dropped across northwest Georgia cities By FOX 5 Atlanta Digital Team FOX 5 Atlanta Georgia Published October 7, 2026 10:10 AM EDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published October 7, 2026 10:10 AM EDT article Oral rabies vaccines (Credit: United States Department of Agriculture) The Brief Federal wildlife officials are dropping rabies vaccine baits across northwest Georgia to stop the spread of raccoon rabies. Helicopters begin dropping baits on Wednesday, Oct. 7, while low-flying airplanes will begin drops around Oct. 20. The fish-scented baits target raccoons across 15 Georgia counties and seven cities to protect public health. ATLANTA - Federal wildlife officials are distributing over 500,000 oral rabies vaccine baits via air drop across northwest Georgia to prevent the disease from spreading. What we know: The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Wildlife Services program is dropping oral rabies vaccine baits across more than 7,000 square kilometers in northwest Georgia. Low-flying airplanes and helicopters are distributing the fish-scented baits to vaccinate raccoons and other wild animals. Helicopters begin baiting cities on Wednesday, Oct. 7, while airplane drops begin around Oct. 20. Helicopter drops will last two to three days, and airplane distribution will take about one week. The aerial baiting targets 15 counties: Bartow, Catoosa, Chattooga, Dade, Floyd, Fannin, Gilmer, Gordon, Murray, Pickens, Rabun, Towns, Union, Walker and Whitfield. Helicopters will specifically cover the cities of Dalton, Lafayette, Rome, Calhoun, Fort Oglethorpe, Chickamauga and Tunnel Hill. The program is part of a nationwide effort to halt the westward movement of raccoon rabies. Federal officials are conducting the operation to address a public health and safety emergency. What you can do: Officials advise leaving intact baits alone so wild animals can find them. If an intact bait is in the open, toss it deeper into the woods using gloves or a towel, then wash your hands immediately. Do not try to take a bait away from a pet, as animals may bite out of instinct. While the baits do not harm pets, eating many of them can cause an upset stomach. Anyone who touches the liquid vaccine inside a bait should wash their hands right away and call their local health department. Questions about the Wildlife Services Oral Rabies Vaccination Program can be directed to the USDA at 1-866-487-3297. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services program, which announced details of the oral rabies vaccination initiative alongside the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Georgia Department of Health. analysis.brief_en: Federal wildlife officials in northwest Georgia are distributing over 500,000 oral rabies vaccine baits via air drops to prevent the spread of raccoon rabies. The operation, which began on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, targets 15 counties and seven cities, covering more than 7,000 square kilometers. news.content: KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WATE) — The Tennessee Department of Health has joined forces with the U.S. Department of Agriculture to combat the spread of rabies by dropping oral rabies vaccine (ORV) baits over five states. The bait distribution program is part of an effort to prevent the spread of the rabies virus by wild animals, most often raccoons, to the west. The ORV bait is coated with fish oil and fishmeal crumbles, which give off a pungent odor and attract raccoons to them. When an animal bites into the bait, the vaccine coats the back of their throat and vaccinates them." RABORAL V-RG® coated sachet oral rabies vaccine baits distributed in Tennessee (Photo via USDA) "We're targeting raccoons because they seem to be an animal that people like to associate with or befriend, shall we say," said Betsy Haley, GIS planner and wildlife biologist for the National Rabies Management Program in USDA. "When [people] feed their animals outside, the raccoons come up, and they think it's cute. Well, by vaccinating the raccoons, we're helping to protect those pets, as well as those pet owners from potential rabies exposure." The USDA said a total of 2.4 million baits will be distributed in east Tennessee, western North Carolina, southwest Virginia, north central Alabama, and north Georgia. In Tennessee, over 200,000 baits will be dropped. Starting October 7 to 12, helicopters will drop baits in urban and suburban communities in Athens, Charleston, Collegedale, Decatur, Elizabethton, Erwin, Johnson City, Mountain City, and Riceville. Then, between October 15-25, low-flying airplanes will drop baits in rural areas in Bradley, Carter, Greene, Hamilton, Johnson, McMinn, Meigs, Polk, Rhea, Sullivan, Unicoi, and Washington counties. Don't approach elk: NPS warning follows injury in Great Smoky Mountains The ORV baits have been distributed in Tennessee since 2002 as part of a larger effort to prevent the westward spread of raccoon rabies by creating a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains from the Canadian border to Alabama. Haley said the program has been very successful in preventing the spread west, with no cases making it through the zone to Knoxville. "We've pushed the raccoon rabies cases back to the very eastern tip there in the north-northeast part of the state as well as some southern areas around Chattanooga and Cleveland area we're still baiting, but for the most part in Tennessee it's working very well," said Haley. Rabies infects the central nervous system, causing inflammation of the brain and eventually death. While the disease is rare in humans, with only 1 to 3 cases reported a year according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it can have serious consequences. The majority of cases are found in wild animals, according to the CDC. "The hopes for these programs are to vaccinate as many raccoons as we can. These vaccine baits will work with other wildlife, but we are specifically targeting raccoons to try to reduce and potentially eliminate raccoon rabies variant from the environment," said Haley. Haley added that raccoons are the most common carrier of rabies in wildlife in the East. Because of this, the USDA asks people not to feed their animals outside and to keep their trash secured to limit contact with raccoons that could be carrying the virus. Could Tennessee try to execute Christa Pike again? Lawyer explains fallout, proposed legal changes The oral rabies vaccine bait packets will also be marked with a toll-free number (1-877-722-6725) for assistance or information if someone finds or comes in contact with a bait packet. "If you find the bait, don't freak out; don't automatically pick it up. If you need to move it, if it's in a spot where, say, it might have accidentally fallen on the sidewalk, or it's right on the edge of your yard, you can either use a paper towel or rubber gloves, pick it up and move it. And we say to do that just because the fish on the outside of the packet really does leave a pungent odor on your fingers," said Haley. Haley added that if a person or their pet comes into contact with the bait, it is not going to harm them. "It may, at worst, get an upset stomach from eating the bait, but don't try to take the bait out of the dog's mouth, because you could potentially expose yourself to the vaccine. And all that would do is potentially give you a rash. So, if you need to take it out of the dog's mouth, wash your hands really well with soap and water and keep an eye on that spot if you do get scratched," said Haley. news.title_zh: 空投 狂犬病 疫苗 如何防止病毒传播到诺克斯维尔
news.source_body_en: The Tennessee Department of Health and the U.S. Department of Agriculture are collaborating to distribute oral rabies vaccine (ORV) baits over five states, including Tennessee, to prevent the westward spread of rabies, particularly from raccoons, into Knoxville. The bait distribution program, which has been ongoing since 2002, aims to create a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains to stop the spread of the raccoon rabies variant. The baits are coated with fish oil and fishmeal crumbles to attract raccoons and are being dropped in urban and suburban areas from October 7 to 12, 2026, and in rural areas from October 15 to 25, 2026. The program has been successful in preventing the spread westward, with no cases making it through the zone to Knoxville. The USDA has emphasized that the baits are safe for humans and pets, and they have provided guidance on handling them to avoid potential exposure. The initiative is part of a broader effort to reduce and potentially eliminate raccoon rabies in the region.
news.content_zh: 田纳西州卫生部和美国农业部正在合作,在包括田纳西州在内的五个州分发口服 狂犬病 疫苗 (ORV) 诱饵,以防止 狂犬病 向西传播,特别是通过浣熊传播到诺克斯维尔。该诱饵分发计划自 2002 年以来一直在进行,旨在沿阿巴拉契亚山脉建立屏障,阻止浣熊 狂犬病 变种的传播。这些诱饵涂有鱼油和鱼粉碎屑以吸引浣熊,将于2026年10月7日至12日在城市和郊区以及2026年10月15日至25日在农村地区投放。该计划成功地阻止了疫情向西蔓延,没有病例穿过该地区到达诺克斯维尔。美国农业部强调,这些诱饵对人类和宠物来说是安全的,并提供了处理这些诱饵的指南,以避免潜在的接触。该举措是减少并可能消除该地区浣熊 狂犬病 的更广泛努力的一部分。

Healthy Living Asheville-Area Families Should Keep Kids and Pets Away From Rabies Vaccine Baits as Helicopter and Airplane Drops Begin Published Oct 07, 2026 10:30 AM EDT By Dorothy Brooks Peter McCabe | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Families in Asheville and three nearby mountain towns may soon find small fishmeal-scented packets in their yards, parks and driveways. Starting Friday, Oct. 9, helicopters will drop oral rabies vaccine baits over greater Asheville, Burnsville, Mars Hill and Waynesville through Oct. 13, according to a North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services news release issued Oct. 5. Low-flying airplanes will then cover 17 western counties from Oct. 15 to 22. The baits are meant for raccoons, but children pick up odd objects and dogs love anything fishy. State officials say an intact bait will not harm people, pets, or wildlife, yet they want households to know what to do if a child or dog gets to one first. One clarification matters: helicopters are used only over those four town areas. Crews began placing baits by hand around Asheville on Oct. 5 through Oct. 9, and the wider rural coverage comes from fixed-wing airplanes. Drop Schedule for Buncombe, Haywood, Yancey and 14 Other Counties The airplane phase, set for Oct. 15 through Oct. 22, covers Ashe, Avery, Buncombe, Cherokee, Clay, Graham, Haywood, Henderson, Jackson, Macon, Madison, McDowell, Mitchell, Swain, Transylvania, Watauga and Yancey counties, NCDHHS said. Because Asheville is in Buncombe County, that county is covered by all three methods this month. NCDHHS and the U.S. Department of Agriculture expect to distribute roughly 600,000 baits in North Carolina this year. The release does not list street-level flight paths or exact times, so residents of the listed areas should check yards and other outdoor spaces. The USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service announced in July that it planned to spread about 4.5 million baits in 2026 across 13 eastern states, from Maine to Alabama. North Carolina's program has run since 2006 as a partnership among USDA Wildlife Services and several state agencies, according to the state's oral rabies vaccine program page. Spotting a Bait Before a Child or Dog Does Most baits used in this program contain the Raboral V-RG vaccine. Per the USDA's oral rabies vaccine page, the vaccine sits in a plastic sachet that is either sprinkled with a fishmeal coating or sealed inside a hard fishmeal-polymer block about the size of a matchbox. The state program page likens it to a ketchup packet, in a white plastic package with pink liquid inside. The fishmeal smell draws raccoons to chew the packet open, and it can attract dogs too. If you or your pet come across a bait, NCDHHS says to leave it where it is. The exception is a bait on a lawn, driveway or other open spot unlikely to attract raccoons. In that case, the state says it can be moved to thicker cover where raccoons are more likely to find it, and pets are less likely to reach it. Wear gloves to pick it up. NCDHHS advises using gloves to throw a broken or ruptured bait in the regular trash. Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water if the packet may have broken open. A Swallowed Bait, a Curious Toddler and the Hotline Number If a child or an adult swallows a bait, the state release tells families to contact their local health department or call the phone number printed on the bait: 1-877-722-6725. Saving that number in a phone during the drop window can save time. NCDHHS says eating a bait won't harm a pet, though eating several could temporarily upset its stomach. The USDA says dogs that eat multiple baits face no long-term health risks. Neither people nor pets can catch rabies from contact with the baits, according to the USDA, and the state program page notes the vaccine contains only a single rabies virus gene, not live rabies virus. The real danger remains rabies itself. In 2025, the North Carolina State Laboratory of Public Health tested nearly 4,000 animals and about 6.5% came back positive, NCDHHS said. Raccoons had the most positive results, followed by skunks. Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild animal should wash the wound and promptly contact a health care professional or the local health department. NCDHHS notes that rabies is almost always fatal in mammals, including people, once symptoms develop. Pet Vaccines Still Do the Heavy Lifting Wildlife baiting is an added barrier, not a replacement for household protection. Dr. Carl Williams, NCDHHS public health veterinarian, said in the release that vaccinated pets remain the best prevention, and that vaccinating animals around the home "adds another layer of protection against the spread of this deadly disease." State law requires dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies by 4 months of age and to stay current afterward. Families who are unsure whether a pet's shot has lapsed can check vaccination records with their veterinarian or ask the county health department whether any low-cost rabies clinics are scheduled. The larger goal reaches beyond the mountains. According to the state program page, the vaccine barrier runs from eastern Ohio down the Appalachian ridge to northeastern Alabama, with the goal of keeping raccoon rabies from spreading into Tennessee. MedicalDaily recently reported a different rabies risk in Southern California, where Los Angeles County's rabid bat count tied a record and health officials urged families finding bats indoors to call a doctor. For western North Carolina households, the next two weeks call for awareness rather than alarm. Healthy Living Asheville-Area Families Should Keep Kids and Pets Away From Rabies Vaccine Baits as Helicopter and Airplane Drops Begin Published Oct 07, 2026 10:30 AM EDT By Dorothy Brooks Peter McCabe | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Families in Asheville and three nearby mountain towns may soon find small fishmeal-scented packets in their yards, parks and driveways. Starting Friday, Oct. 9, helicopters will drop oral rabies vaccine baits over greater Asheville, Burnsville, Mars Hill and Waynesville through Oct. 13, according to a North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services news release issued Oct. 5. Low-flying airplanes will then cover 17 western counties from Oct. 15 to 22. The baits are meant for raccoons, but children pick up odd objects and dogs love anything fishy. State officials say an intact bait will not harm people, pets, or wildlife, yet they want households to know what to do if a child or dog gets to one first. One clarification matters: helicopters are used only over those four town areas. Crews began placing baits by hand around Asheville on Oct. 5 through Oct. 9, and the wider rural coverage comes from fixed-wing airplanes. Drop Schedule for Buncombe, Haywood, Yancey and 14 Other Counties The airplane phase, set for Oct. 15 through Oct. 22, covers Ashe, Avery, Buncombe, Cherokee, Clay, Graham, Haywood, Henderson, Jackson, Macon, Madison, McDowell, Mitchell, Swain, Transylvania, Watauga and Yancey counties, NCDHHS said. Because Asheville is in Buncombe County, that county is covered by all three methods this month. NCDHHS and the U.S. Department of Agriculture expect to distribute roughly 600,000 baits in North Carolina this year. The release does not list street-level flight paths or exact times, so residents of the listed areas should check yards and other outdoor spaces. The USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service announced in July that it planned to spread about 4.5 million baits in 2026 across 13 eastern states, from Maine to Alabama. North Carolina's program has run since 2006 as a partnership among USDA Wildlife Services and several state agencies, according to the state's oral rabies vaccine program page. Spotting a Bait Before a Child or Dog Does Most baits used in this program contain the Raboral V-RG vaccine. Per the USDA's oral rabies vaccine page, the vaccine sits in a plastic sachet that is either sprinkled with a fishmeal coating or sealed inside a hard fishmeal-polymer block about the size of a matchbox. The state program page likens it to a ketchup packet, in a white plastic package with pink liquid inside. The fishmeal smell draws raccoons to chew the packet open, and it can attract dogs too. If you or your pet come across a bait, NCDHHS says to leave it where it is. The exception is a bait on a lawn, driveway or other open spot unlikely to attract raccoons. In that case, the state says it can be moved to thicker cover where raccoons are more likely to find it, and pets are less likely to reach it. Wear gloves to pick it up. NCDHHS advises using gloves to throw a broken or ruptured bait in the regular trash. Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water if the packet may have broken open. A Swallowed Bait, a Curious Toddler and the Hotline Number If a child or an adult swallows a bait, the state release tells families to contact their local health department or call the phone number printed on the bait: 1-877-722-6725. Saving that number in a phone during the drop window can save time. NCDHHS says eating a bait won't harm a pet, though eating several could temporarily upset its stomach. The USDA says dogs that eat multiple baits face no long-term health risks. Neither people nor pets can catch rabies from contact with the baits, according to the USDA, and the state program page notes the vaccine contains only a single rabies virus gene, not live rabies virus. The real danger remains rabies itself. In 2025, the North Carolina State Laboratory of Public Health tested nearly 4,000 animals and about 6.5% came back positive, NCDHHS said. Raccoons had the most positive results, followed by skunks. Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild animal should wash the wound and promptly contact a health care professional or the local health department. NCDHHS notes that rabies is almost always fatal in mammals, including people, once symptoms develop. Pet Vaccines Still Do the Heavy Lifting Wildlife baiting is an added barrier, not a replacement for household protection. Dr. Carl Williams, NCDHHS public health veterinarian, said in the release that vaccinated pets remain the best prevention, and that vaccinating animals around the home "adds another layer of protection against the spread of this deadly disease." State law requires dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies by 4 months of age and to stay current afterward. Families who are unsure whether a pet's shot has lapsed can check vaccination records with their veterinarian or ask the county health department whether any low-cost rabies clinics are scheduled. The larger goal reaches beyond the mountains. According to the state program page, the vaccine barrier runs from eastern Ohio down the Appalachian ridge to northeastern Alabama, with the goal of keeping raccoon rabies from spreading into Tennessee. MedicalDaily recently reported a different rabies risk in Southern California, where Los Angeles County's rabid bat count tied a record and health officials urged families finding bats indoors to call a doctor. For western North Carolina households, the next two weeks call for awareness rather than alarm. Look around before letting toddlers or dogs out, leave intact baits alone or move them with gloves, and keep the 1-877-722-6725 number handy until the airplane phase ends Oct. 22. Questions about a bite, scratch, or swallowed bait should go to a clinician or the local health department. news.content: Saturday, October 10, 2026 Menu #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Search #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Menu FG seeks responsible pet ownership, vaccination to prevent human deaths from dog-triggered rabies The statement noted that the WHO would support Nigeria in rabies investigations and response coordination. ADEFEMOLA AKINTADE • October 8, 2026 Rottweiler and Alsatian The Nigerian government has advocated responsible animal ownership, urging dog owners to ensure their pets are vaccinated from time-to-time. The call was made during a sensitisation campaign aimed at ending human deaths from dog-triggered rabies by 2030. Rabies is largely contracted from dog saliva when it makes contact with broken skin or injuries which attacks the body’s central nervous system. The Federal Ministry of Livestock Development said it recorded over a 100 cases of animal rabies across 16 states between January and August 2026, highlighting the rampancy of the disease in the nation. “Protecting communities from rabies requires everyone to play a part. We must stop working in silos and continue to educate families, encourage responsible animal ownership, and work together to reduce risks in our communities,” Chinyere Ijeoma Akujobi, permanent secretary, Federal Ministry of Livestock Development, said in a statement on Thursday. Nigeria has adopted One Health approach combining human, animal and environmental health sectors to combat rabies. One Health officer at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Dorcas Mernyi, called for prompt treatment in the event of exposure. She said, “No one should die from rabies simply because they did not know what to do after a dog bite or could not access treatment. We must ensure health workers recognise possible exposure immediately and that patients receive appropriate care without delay.” The WHO Emergency Preparedness and Response Cluster Lead in Nigeria, Alexander Chimbaru, says death prevention was team work requiring cooperation of all citizens. “Ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies requires sustained collaboration between government, health and veterinary professionals, communities and dog owners. Every dog vaccinated, every exposure reported early and every person who receives timely care takes us closer to the 2030 goal,” Mr Chimbaru said. The statement noted that the World Health Organisation would support Nigeria in rabies investigations and response coordination. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention advised victims of animal bites and scratches to immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for a minimum of 15 minutes and urgently seek health care. The centre urged victims not to wait for symptoms to appear before seeking treatment. analysis.brief_en: The Nigerian government, through the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development, has called for responsible pet ownership and vaccination to prevent human deaths from dog-triggered rabies. This initiative is part of a broader sensitisation campaign aimed at ending such deaths by 2030. Between January and August 2026, the ministry recorded over 100 cases of animal rabies across 16 states, highlighting the disease's prevalence. Rabies, contracted from dog saliva, attacks the central nervous system and can be fatal if not treated promptly. This initiative is part of a broader sensitisation campaign aimed at ending such deaths by 2030. Between January and August 2026, the ministry recorded over 100 cases of animal rabies across 16 states, highlighting the disease's prevalence. Rabies, contracted from dog saliva, attacks the central nervous system and can be fatal if not treated promptly. The WHO has pledged support for rabies investigations and response coordination in Nigeria. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention has advised victims of animal bites to wash wounds immediately with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent healthcare without delay. The government is promoting a One Health approach, combining human, animal, and environmental health sectors, to combat rabies effectively. This effort requires sustained collaboration between government, health professionals, communities, and dog owners to reduce risks and achieve the 2030 goal.
news.content_zh: 尼日利亚政府通过联邦畜牧业发展部呼吁负责任的宠物饲养和 疫苗接种,以防止因狗引发的 狂犬病 造成人类死亡。这项举措是旨在到 2030 年消除此类死亡的更广泛宣传活动的一部分。2026 年 1 月至 8 月期间,该部在 16 个州记录了 100 多例动物 狂犬病 病例,强调了该疾病的 狂犬病。狂犬病 由狗唾液感染,会攻击中枢神经系统,如果不及时治疗可能致命。世界卫生组织已承诺支持尼日利亚的 狂犬病 调查和应对协调。尼日利亚疾病控制和预防中心建议动物咬伤受害者立即用肥皂和流水清洗伤口至少15分钟,并立即寻求紧急医疗护理。政府正在推广“同一个健康”方法,将人类、动物和环境卫生部门结合起来,以有效对抗 狂犬病。这项努力需要政府、卫生专业人员、社区和狗主人之间的持续合作,以降低风险并实现 2030 年目标。

news.content: From bite to fatal disease: The rabies threat/HILLARY BETT Rabies is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that affects the central nervous system and is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms appear. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that rabies causes about 59,000 human deaths each year in more than 150 countries, with about 95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia. Children account for approximately 40% of human rabies deaths. Dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies cases, with the virus transmitted mainly through bites and scratches from infected animals. Early symptoms can include fever, pain and unusual tingling or burning at the wound site. As the disease progresses, it can cause severe inflammation of the brain and spinal cord. Rabies deaths are preventable through mass vaccination of dogs and timely post-exposure prophylaxis. People bitten or scratched by a potentially infected animal should immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical care

A bat in a village near Baniyas, Tartous countryside (western Syria), an area known for its widespread populations of cave-dwelling bats and Kuhl's pipistrelle, January 21, 2024 (Syrian Wildlife Enthusiasts/Facebook). Enab Baladi 09/10/2026 7:53 pm Society A A A هل تقف الخفافيش وراء إصابات "داء الكلب" في سوريا؟ Syrian governorates have witnessed a marked rise in rabies cases, with the number of people potentially exposed to the virus increasing by 62.7% in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period the previous year. The threat has not been limited to humans. Still, it has also affected the livestock sector, with sporadic viral outbreaks, most recently in the western Raqqa countryside (northeastern Syria) and orchards surrounding the city of Homs (central Syria). These outbreaks have caused economic losses as livestock have died or had to be culled and disposed of according to sanitary procedures. The outbreaks have coincided with the spread of local accounts attributing the disease primarily to bat attacks, sparking widespread debate over whether this explanation is scientifically accurate and supported by the facts. How the Rabies Virus Spreads Dr. Fahem Abdalaziz, professor of microbiology at the Faculty of Medicine at Tartous University, confirmed that rabies is an acute, fatal viral infection affecting the central nervous system. It is transmitted to humans and domestic animals through the saliva of infected animals. Speaking to Enab Baladi, the specialist explained that rabies, also known as hydrophobia, is considered one of the most dangerous viral diseases because it is nearly 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear. However, Abdalaziz emphasized that despite the disease’s extreme severity, a crucial preventive option exists: death can be prevented and the disease avoided through the timely administration of vaccines and appropriate medical treatments. Discussing the epidemiological characteristics of rabies, Abdalaziz explained that it is classified as a zoonotic disease, with a wide range of wild animals, including foxes, raccoons, squirrels, and bats, as well as domestic animals such as dogs and cats, serving as reservoirs of the deadly virus. Regarding transmission, the microbiology professor said humans are usually infected through bites, although transmission can occur in rarer circumstances through the inhalation of airborne droplets contaminated with the virus. From a biological perspective, Abdalaziz described the virus’s progression through the body, explaining that once infection occurs, it travels along nerve pathways in the peripheral nervous system. He added that the retrograde axonal transport of the virus to the central nervous system is the key process underlying the development of natural infection and disease. This explains the severe risks involved and the critical importance of vaccination before it is too late. Bats: The Mystery of Unexplained Cases and Silent Transmission Expanding on his analysis of how the disease spreads, Abdalaziz noted that recent years have seen a surge in scientific studies examining how rabies is transmitted specifically from bats to humans, particularly following mysterious deaths involving people who had no obvious bite, scratch, or even contact considered dangerous. Based on these findings, the microbiology professor explained that recent research has shown that the danger is not limited to a bite in the conventional sense. The virus can also be transmitted through seemingly minor direct contact that leaves no visible mark on the skin. Abdalaziz attributed the danger of this type of exposure to bats’ extremely fine, sharp teeth, which can cause microscopic wounds that go unnoticed, explaining why some infected people do not realize they have been exposed. Regarding the role of bats in spreading the disease, the specialist said recent laboratory analyses have demonstrated that bats are not merely incidental carriers of the virus but natural reservoirs in which it can persist. This increases the possibility of transmission through direct contact, even when no wounds are visible. To illustrate these findings, the specialist cited several documented examples of exposure and infection identified in scientific research: Underestimating bats inside homes: Cases have been recorded involving people who found bats inside their homes but took no preventive medical measures because they had not noticed a bite or scratch. Days or weeks later, symptoms appeared and rapidly progressed to death. Unprotected direct handling: Researchers documented cases involving people who deliberately picked up bats with their bare hands to remove them or return them to the wild. Although they reported no injuries, subsequent tests confirmed that the bats were carrying the virus. Unnoticed exposure during sleep: Cases have been documented in which a bat was present in a room with a sleeping person. Medical professionals now classify such situations as potentially high-risk exposure requiring immediate assessment and intervention. Refusal of preventive treatment: Tragic cases have been recorded involving people who refused post-exposure preventive treatment even after laboratory tests confirmed that a bat they had encountered was infected. Believing medical intervention was unnecessary, they subsequently died. Local Bat Species: Can They Transmit the Virus? Discussing the specifics of bat-related transmission, Abdalaziz pointed out that international studies and regional statistics indicate that the prevalence of rabies infection among bats is extremely low, at less than 1%. He explained that bats are major reservoirs of the disease, particularly in North and Latin America. Despite the relatively low likelihood of infection locally, the specialist stressed the need for extreme caution following any direct bite or scratch from a bat, particularly one that cannot fly or displays unusual behavior. Bat teeth are extremely fine, and people may not notice being bitten or scratched while sleeping or during close contact. Regarding their characteristics and distribution, the microbiology professor explained that bats are flying mammals whose heads resemble those of dogs. Syria is home to several species of different sizes, inhabiting caves, grottoes, forests, and coastal areas. The most prominent include: Kuhl’s pipistrelle: A small bat found in plains and low-lying areas, including Syria’s coastal region, particularly Latakia, Tartous, and Baniyas, as well as humid inland areas. The Arabian or Levantine noctule: A nocturnal bat found in Levantine environments, temperate forests, and caves. The desert long-eared bat: A species inhabiting desert and arid environments in Syria and the wider Middle East. Fruit bats and cave-dwelling bats: These are common in limestone caves and rocky grottoes across the mountains and plains of Syria’s coastal region, where the environment provides shelter and food from fruit trees such as figs, pomegranates, and stone-fruit trees. Abdalaziz reassured residents that most bat species native to Syria feed on insects or fruit, and that the country has no vampire bats that feed on the blood of living animals. However, he cautioned that bats can contract rabies in the same way as other mammals, through exposure to the infected saliva of another animal, such as another bat, a fox, or a wild animal carrying the virus. The virus can also spread within bat colonies through close contact or shared, confined roosting spaces. Concluding this section, Abdalaziz issued a firm preventive recommendation, emphasizing that despite the low probability of infection in Syria, people should avoid contact with bats altogether. Under no circumstances should they directly handle or pick up a live or dead bat with their bare hands. Other Animals Under Suspicion Regarding the routes of transmission, Abdalaziz explained that rabies is usually transmitted to humans through a bite or deep skin scratch from an infected animal. Infection can also occur when virus-contaminated saliva comes into direct contact with human mucous membranes, such as the eyes or mouth, or with fresh wounds. The microbiology professor explained that dogs are the primary host and transmitter of rabies, accounting for approximately 99% of human rabies cases worldwide. Other potential carriers include carnivorous animals such as hyenas, foxes, wolves, and cats, as well as bats and monkeys. Regarding the virus’s progression through the body, the specialist explained that it enters tissues and peripheral nerves at the site of exposure through infected saliva, then travels slowly along the nerves until it reaches the central nervous system and brain. Once it reaches the brain and multiplies, it spreads to the salivary glands, allowing the infected animal to transmit the virus to another through biting or contact with its saliva. From Gray Matter to the Salivary Glands Turning to the complex mechanisms through which the disease develops inside the body, Abdalaziz described the virus’s progression following infection. He explained that the virus may initially replicate locally after inoculation into the body before traveling to the brain through the axoplasm of peripheral neurons, where it replicates and develops within the gray matter. It then spreads outward through the autonomic nerves to other organs. According to the specialist, this process can lead to infection of the lungs, kidneys, adrenal medulla, and salivary glands. He explained that the presence of the virus in saliva at this stage is the scientific reason an infected animal can transmit the disease through a bite. Regarding the time between exposure and the appearance of symptoms, he noted that the incubation period varies considerably between individuals, depending on the host’s resistance, the amount of virus transmitted, and the distance between the initial site of infection and the central nervous system. The microbiology professor said the incubation period typically ranges from one to eight weeks but can, in unusual cases, extend to several months or even years after exposure. He stressed that this makes it essential not to underestimate any suspicious contact with animals capable of transmitting the disease. Furious and Paralytic Rabies: Clinical Forms of the Disease The microbiology professor described the clinical manifestations of rabies in humans, explaining that the disease typically begins with unusual sensations and tingling at the bite site before rapidly progressing to fatal encephalitis and severe neuronal degeneration in the brain and spinal cord. He added that early symptoms initially resemble influenza, including fever, headache, general fatigue, and numbness or severe itching at the bite site. The disease then progresses into one of two main clinical forms: Furious rabies: Symptoms rapidly develop into hyperactivity, severe agitation, and hydrophobia, accompanied by episodes of terror, hallucinations, and delirium. Death follows within a few days, usually as a result of acute cardiorespiratory failure. Paralytic rabies: This form progresses more slowly and presents with less pronounced symptoms than furious rabies. Muscles gradually become paralyzed, beginning at the site of the bite or scratch. The condition then slowly progresses to complete coma, followed ultimately by death. Abdalaziz noted that paralytic rabies is frequently misdiagnosed, contributing significantly to the underreporting of the disease’s actual prevalence. The specialist also highlighted a fundamental difference in how symptoms appear in different animals. Unlike some other species, an infected bat may not exhibit obvious agitation or aggression. Instead, it may display unusual behavior or movements, such as flying during daylight hours, suddenly falling to the ground, or being unable to fly. Such signs require the public to exercise extreme caution and avoid approaching these animals. The First Lifeline The microbiology professor outlined available medical measures for treatment and prevention, emphasizing that no effective treatment exists once clinical symptoms of rabies have appeared. At the same time, he stressed that immediate, early medical intervention offers the only reliable means of preventing the disease from developing. Regarding first aid, the specialist explained that washing the affected area as quickly as possible with soap and water and thoroughly cleaning the wound can significantly reduce the number of viral particles at the exposure site. He also recommended using a disinfectant capable of inactivating the virus, such as povidone-iodine, iodine tincture, aqueous iodine solution, or ethanol. If mucous membranes, including the eyes, nose, or mouth, have been exposed to the virus, they should be thoroughly rinsed with water without delay. Beyond these immediate measures, Abdalaziz emphasized that effective prevention requires seeking appropriate medical care and visiting a healthcare facility immediately to receive the rabies vaccine and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin as soon as possible, before any clinical symptoms develop. Regarding preventive immunization, the microbiology professor noted that inactivated rabies vaccines are available, including the human diploid cell vaccine used in the United States. He explained that vaccination can also be administered before exposure to individuals considered at high risk because of their occupations, such as veterinarians and dog breeders. Between Mandatory Vaccination and the Lack of Government Support Veterinarian Abdul Basit Wakiyeh, a specialist in ruminant diseases and surgery, expressed regret over the current situation in comments to Enab Baladi, noting that previous governments had provided medicines and antiserums for communicable and infectious diseases. According to Wakiyeh, government medical centers currently lack the necessary antiserums and vaccines, forcing residents to purchase them at their own expense, often from unreliable sources where neither their effectiveness nor their storage conditions can be verified. He added that vaccines for immunizing animals are not available in Syria in the first place. Domestic animals are therefore not routinely vaccinated locally, even in areas classified as severe disease hotspots. The veterinarian also warned about the dangerous state of slaughterhouses in Syria, describing their conditions as “backward” because they lack specialized laboratories and mechanisms for collecting samples for analysis. Instead, inspections rely solely on visual examination, which he stressed is entirely insufficient to detect serious diseases. In this context, Wakiyeh warned that the absence of laboratory oversight allows unscrupulous individuals to pass infected meat into the market. Regarding first aid, the specialist explained that washing the affected area as quickly as possible with soap and water and thoroughly cleaning the wound can significantly reduce the number of viral particles at the exposure site. He also recommended using a disinfectant capable of inactivating the virus, such as povidone-iodine, iodine tincture, aqueous iodine solution, or ethanol. If mucous membranes, including the eyes, nose, or mouth, have been exposed to the virus, they should be thoroughly rinsed with water without delay. Beyond these immediate measures, Abdalaziz emphasized that effective prevention requires seeking appropriate medical care and visiting a healthcare facility immediately to receive the rabies vaccine and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin as soon as possible, before any clinical symptoms develop. Regarding preventive immunization, the microbiology professor noted that inactivated rabies vaccines are available, including the human diploid cell vaccine used in the United States. He explained that vaccination can also be administered before exposure to individuals considered at high risk because of their occupations, such as veterinarians and dog breeders. Between Mandatory Vaccination and the Lack of Government Support Veterinarian Abdul Basit Wakiyeh, a specialist in ruminant diseases and surgery, expressed regret over the current situation in comments to Enab Baladi, noting that previous governments had provided medicines and antiserums for communicable and infectious diseases. According to Wakiyeh, government medical centers currently lack the necessary antiserums and vaccines, forcing residents to purchase them at their own expense, often from unreliable sources where neither their effectiveness nor their storage conditions can be verified. He added that vaccines for immunizing animals are not available in Syria in the first place. Domestic animals are therefore not routinely vaccinated locally, even in areas classified as severe disease hotspots. The veterinarian also warned about the dangerous state of slaughterhouses in Syria, describing their conditions as “backward” because they lack specialized laboratories and mechanisms for collecting samples for analysis. Instead, inspections rely solely on visual examination, which he stressed is entirely insufficient to detect serious diseases. In this context, Wakiyeh warned that the absence of laboratory oversight allows unscrupulous individuals to pass infected meat into the market. Set us as preferred Los Angeles County health officials are reminding residents and their pets to be safe around wild animals, after finding the first rabid raccoon case in more than 50 years. A sick raccoon was discovered in a Westlake Village backyard but was not aggressive toward people, behavior that is commonly associated with rabies-infected animals, the Los Angeles County Public Health Department announced Monday. A few people at a worksite near the animal and a dog — that was up to date on its rabies vaccination — were potentially exposed to the disease. Advertisement “The detection of rabies in a raccoon is an important reminder to never touch, handle or feed any wild animals, even when they appear healthy,” said Dr. Muntu Davis, health officer for Los Angeles County. “Always keep a safe distance from wildlife and contact your local animal control if you encounter an animal that appears sick, injured or is behaving unusually.” Four people at the worksite are receiving rabies post-exposure prophylaxis — which can include a dose of human rabies immune globulin and a rabies vaccine, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The canine is under quarantine and officials say it’s doing well. Rabies is a rare but serious disease that can infect the brains of both people and animals, according to the California Department of Public Health. Advertisement An infected animal can pass rabies to another animal or to a person through its bite, but that’s not the only way it can be transmitted. Exposure can occur any time saliva or tissue from the infected animal enters the body, such as through a bite or a scratch, or contact with a wound or the mouth, nose or eyes. In California, bats and skunks are the animals that most often get rabies, according to the state health department. The last known rabid raccoon in Los Angeles County was detected in 1973, when a skunk variant of rabies was still present in the area. That particular strain has not been detected in the county since 1979. Officials say the last animal confirmed to have rabies that wasn’t a bat was a skunk infected with the bat strain of rabies in Long Beach in 2014. Public health officials are investigating which rabies strain the raccoon was infected with. Advertisement “Based on current knowledge of rabies occurrence in Los Angeles County, it is likely this raccoon was infected with rabies from a bat,” public health officials stated in a news release. “However, Public Health is awaiting subsequent variant testing, which can take several weeks.” Rabies exposure in L.A. County is more commonly linked to rabies-infected bats. Rabid bat detections can vary year-to-year, but Los Angeles County has seen a steady upward trend for more than a decade. So far this year, there have been a record-breaking 70 rabid bats confirmed in Los Angeles County. Experts who study bats say that, although residents should practice caution, the odds of getting rabies from the flying creatures remain very low. A sick raccoon was discovered in a Westlake Village backyard but was not aggressive toward people, behavior that is commonly associated with rabies-infected animals, the Los Angeles County Public Health Department announced Monday. A few people at a worksite near the animal and a dog — that was up to date on its rabies vaccination — were potentially exposed to the disease. Advertisement “The detection of rabies in a raccoon is an important reminder to never touch, handle or feed any wild animals, even when they appear healthy,” said Dr. Muntu Davis, health officer for Los Angeles County. “Always keep a safe distance from wildlife and contact your local animal control if you encounter an animal that appears sick, injured or is behaving unusually.” Four people at the worksite are receiving rabies post-exposure prophylaxis — which can include a dose of human rabies immune globulin and a rabies vaccine, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The canine is under quarantine and officials say it’s doing well. Rabies is a rare but serious disease that can infect the brains of both people and animals, according to the California Department of Public Health. Advertisement An infected animal can pass rabies to another animal or to a person through its bite, but that’s not the only way it can be transmitted. Exposure can occur any time saliva or tissue from the infected animal enters the body, such as through a bite or a scratch, or contact with a wound or the mouth, nose or eyes. In California, bats and skunks are the animals that most often get rabies, according to the state health department. The last known rabid raccoon in Los Angeles County was detected in 1973, when a skunk variant of rabies was still present in the area. That particular strain has not been detected in the county since 1979. Officials say the last animal confirmed to have rabies that wasn’t a bat was a skunk infected with the bat strain of rabies in Long Beach in 2014. Public health officials are investigating which rabies strain the raccoon was infected with. Advertisement “Based on current knowledge of rabies occurrence in Los Angeles County, it is likely this raccoon was infected with rabies from a bat,” public health officials stated in a news release. “However, Public Health is awaiting subsequent variant testing, which can take several weeks.” Rabies exposure in L.A. Experts who study bats say that, although residents should practice caution, the odds of getting rabies from the flying creatures remain very low. Rabies infects very few humans in the United States and California, according to the state public health department. Fewer than 10 human deaths are reported each year in the nation. news.content: Skip to main content Download the AppGet your news faster with our mobile experience Install News Weather Sports Chime In Money Watch Live Now 76° Sat 62° Sun 71° Sign In or Create Account Watch Rockingham County animal shelter to offer free rabies shots Oct. 30 by Kristen Moorhead Tue, October 6, 2026 at 3:41 PM Rockingham County animal shelter to offer free rabies shots Oct. 30 0Comment Share topics: Rabies Free vaccinations Animal shelter Rockingham County Reidsville Rabies clinic Pet owners North Carolina law ROCKINGHAM COUNTY, N.C. — Pet owners in Rockingham County will have a chance to protect their animals against a deadly disease at no cost later this month. The Rockingham County Animal Shelter will offer free one-year rabies vaccinations for dogs and cats on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Vaccinations will be available at the shelter at 250 Cherokee Camp Road in Reidsville from 9 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. and from 1 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of mammals, including dogs, cats, wildlife and humans. It is most commonly spread through the bite of an infected animal. Once symptoms develop, rabies is almost always fatal, making vaccination critical for prevention. Wild animals such as raccoons, skunks, foxes and bats can carry rabies and expose pets and people to the virus. The shelter noted that even pets that spend most of their time indoors can still encounter wildlife, so keeping vaccinations current adds an important layer of protection. BE THE FIRST TO COMMENT North Carolina law requires owners of dogs, cats and ferrets 4 months of age and older to keep their animals currently vaccinated against rabies. Pet owners are encouraged to take advantage of the free clinic to make sure their animals are protected. news.content_zh: 北卡罗来纳州里兹维尔的罗金厄姆县动物收容所将于 2026 年 10 月 30 日星期五为狗和猫免费提供一年期的 狂犬病 狂犬病。这一举措是北卡罗来纳州法律的一部分,该法律要求宠物主人为其动物接种 狂犬病 疫苗。狂犬病 是一种致命的病毒性疾病,影响哺乳动物(包括宠物和人类)的神经系统,最常见的是通过受感染动物的叮咬传播。该庇护所指出,即使是室内宠物也可能遇到野生动物,因此 疫苗接种 对于预防至关重要。一旦出现症状,狂犬病 几乎总是致命的,因此保持 狂犬病 处于最新状态至关重要。该事件已得到证实,尚未接受调查,收容所积极推广诊所,以确保社区保护。

news.title: Mass Dog Vaccination Drive in Ghanaian City Reaches 70% Coverage Against Rabies
news.excerpt: An evaluation of a One Health-coordinated mass dog rabies vaccination campaign in Techiman, Ghana, found an estimated 70 percent coverage alongside key logistical barriers.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 10, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Mass Dog Vaccination Drive in Ghanaian City Reaches 70% Coverage Against Rabies by October 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Mass Dog Vaccination Drive in Ghanaian City Reaches 70% Coverage Against Rabies Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A free mass dog vaccination campaign in Techiman South Metropolitan, Ghana, has achieved an estimated 70 percent coverage of the city’s dog population, meeting the internationally recommended threshold needed to interrupt rabies transmission, according to a new evaluation published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. The campaign, coordinated under a One Health framework and carried out in September 2024, offers one of the few detailed operational assessments of a municipal-level dog vaccination effort in a rapidly urbanizing, resource-constrained setting in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its findings carry weight far beyond Techiman, because rabies still kills an estimated tens of thousands of people each year worldwide, with the overwhelming majority of human cases linked to bites from infected dogs. The evaluation team, led by Prince Kyere Dwaah of institutions in Ghana, conducted a mixed-methods post-campaign assessment two weeks after the vaccination drive ended. The design combined quantitative and qualitative strands. Quantitative data came from structured questionnaires administered to 200 dog-owning households, alongside a review of administrative vaccination records used to estimate overall coverage. Qualitative data came from key informant interviews with the people who actually delivered the campaign: veterinary officers, public health professionals, environmental health personnel, and community leaders. Descriptive statistics summarized household participation and awareness indicators, while the interview material was analyzed thematically to identify what helped and what hindered implementation. The household survey revealed important details about the structure of dog ownership in Techiman. Among the surveyed households, 59.5 percent owned more than one dog, a pattern that matters for campaign planning because multi-dog households can amplify both transmission risk and the logistical burden of reaching every animal. Just over half of the households, 51.5 percent, reported vaccinating at least one dog during the campaign. That figure, while substantial, also signals that nearly half of the dog-owning households surveyed did not participate, a gap the authors link to the operational barriers documented elsewhere in the study. Perhaps the most striking results concern rabies knowledge. Awareness that rabies is fatal rose from 45 percent, based on self-reported recall of pre-campaign knowledge, to 75 percent after the campaign period. Awareness that rabies is preventable increased from 40 percent to 70 percent. These are self-reported figures and therefore subject to recall and social desirability biases, but the magnitude of the shifts suggests that the campaign’s public communication component, including mobilization around World Rabies Day, reached a large share of the community. Because demand for vaccination depends heavily on owners understanding the stakes, this knowledge gain is not merely a soft outcome; it is a structural ingredient of coverage. On the supply side, administrative records indicated that approximately 5,600 dogs were vaccinated during the campaign. When set against projected dog population figures for the metropolitan area, this corresponds to an estimated 70 percent coverage, exactly the threshold that the World Health Organization and partner agencies have long identified as necessary to break the transmission cycle of canine rabies. The technical logic behind that threshold is rooted in the basic reproduction number of rabies in dog populations: if a sufficiently large fraction of dogs is immune at any given time, each infectious dog fails to transmit the virus onward often enough to sustain the epidemic, and the pathogen dies out locally. Sustaining that level year after year, however, is considerably harder than reaching it once. The evaluation was careful to distinguish administrative coverage from effective population immunity. Administrative figures count doses delivered at fixed points and outreach stations, but they can overstate true immunity if dogs are missed unevenly across neighborhoods, if records are incomplete, or if free-roaming animals are systematically excluded. In Techiman, the qualitative interviews surfaced precisely such concerns. Participants identified strong multisectoral collaboration and World Rabies Day mobilization as key facilitators of the campaign, evidence that the One Health approach, which deliberately links human, animal, and environmental health sectors, can translate into concrete operational gains when it is built into campaign design from the start. Against those facilitators stood a set of persistent barriers that the authors argue could undermine effective immunity even when headline coverage looks adequate. Vaccine supply delays disrupted planning and delivery. Cold-chain capacity was limited, a critical weakness because rabies vaccines are thermolabile; if the cold chain breaks, doses may lose potency before they are injected, silently eroding protection. Access was inadequate for peri-urban communities, the fast-growing fringe zones where dog populations are often dense and veterinary services thin. And the campaign lacked strategies for vaccinating free-roaming dogs, a population that fixed-point vaccination inherently struggles to reach because unowned and loosely owned animals rarely present themselves at posts. In many African cities, free-roaming dogs make up a substantial share of the total population, so their exclusion can leave a reservoir of susceptible animals even in a nominally well-covered district. These findings sit within a broader and well-documented pattern across Sub-Saharan Africa, where mass dog vaccination programmes are frequently constrained not by the complete unavailability of vaccines but by inconsistent procurement, financing limitations, cold-chain requirements, and weaknesses in distribution systems. The Techiman study contributes operational evidence from a municipal campaign, a scale that has been underrepresented in the literature compared with national programme reviews or small pilot projects. Rapidly urbanizing cities like Techiman present a distinctive epidemiological profile: growing human populations, expanding peri-urban settlements, dense dog ownership, and health infrastructure stretched across jurisdictional boundaries. Campaign models that work in rural districts may not transfer cleanly to such settings, which is why locally grounded evaluations like this one matter for regional policy. The authors draw a set of practical conclusions for future campaigns. Vaccine logistics need strengthening, with procurement timed to avoid delays and cold-chain capacity expanded so that potency is preserved from warehouse to injection site. Access for peri-urban communities must be deliberately engineered, for example through satellite stations or mobile teams rather than relying on owners to travel to central points. Monitoring systems should be improved so that coverage estimates can be validated against independent surveys rather than resting solely on administrative counts. Most consequentially, campaigns need to incorporate explicit strategies for free-roaming dogs, which may include catch-vaccinate-release operations, community-based dog population management, and incentives that bring loosely owned animals within reach of vaccinators. The significance of the Techiman evaluation extends to the global goal of eliminating dog-mediated human rabies deaths, a target that international agencies have set for 2030 under the framework Zero by 30. The arithmetic of that goal is unforgiving: every endemic country must reach and sustain at least 70 percent dog vaccination coverage, year after year, in every district. Techiman shows that a resource-constrained African municipality can hit the threshold in a single campaign when sectors collaborate and communities are mobilized. It equally shows that hitting the number once is not the same as controlling the disease, and that the unglamorous machinery of supply chains, cold boxes, peri-urban outreach, and free-roaming dog strategies will determine whether campaigns like this one become the beginning of elimination or a one-off success. The evaluation’s message to programme planners is therefore twofold: celebrate the 70 percent, then get back to work on the barriers that stand between a vaccinated record and a protected population. news.title_original: Mass Dog Vaccination Drive in Ghanaian City Reaches 70% Coverage Against Rabies

analysis.time: The mass dog vaccination drive in Techiman South Metropolitan, Ghana, was conducted in September 2024, with the evaluation published on October 10, 2026. The campaign's post-campaign assessment was conducted two weeks after the drive ended.
analysis.location_and_population: The campaign took place in Techiman South Metropolitan, Ghana, targeting the city's dog population. The evaluation included 200 dog-owning households and estimated the coverage of approximately 5,600 dogs, which corresponds to an estimated 70% of the city's dog population.
analysis.event: A mass dog vaccination campaign in Techiman South Metropolitan, Ghana, achieved 70% coverage of the city’s dog population, meeting the internationally recommended threshold to interrupt rabies transmission. The campaign was coordinated under a One Health framework and included both quantitative and qualitative assessments.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The campaign's 70% coverage aligns with the World Health Organization's threshold for breaking the transmission cycle of canine rabies. However, the evaluation highlights that administrative coverage may not reflect true population immunity due to potential gaps in reaching free-roaming dogs and uneven distribution. The study also notes that rabies remains a significant public health threat, with most human cases linked to dog bites.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The evaluation team conducted a mixed-methods post-campaign assessment, including structured questionnaires and key informant interviews. The findings suggest that while the campaign met the coverage threshold, challenges such as vaccine supply delays, cold-chain limitations, and inadequate access for peri-urban communities may affect long-term effectiveness. The study recommends improving vaccine logistics, access for peri-urban areas, and strategies for free-roaming dogs to ensure sustained immunity.

analysis.brief_en: A mass dog vaccination campaign in Techiman South Metropolitan, Ghana, achieved 70% coverage of the city’s dog population, meeting the internationally recommended threshold to interrupt rabies transmission. The campaign, conducted in September 2024, was evaluated two weeks after its completion and found to be effective in raising awareness about rabies, with 75% of households reporting increased knowledge of its fatality and 70% recognizing its preventability. However, the evaluation also identified challenges, including vaccine supply delays, limited cold-chain capacity, and inadequate access for peri-urban communities. These issues may hinder the campaign’s long-term success, as administrative records may overstate true immunity due to missed dogs in certain areas. The study emphasizes the need for improved logistics, better access strategies, and targeted efforts to reach free-roaming dogs to ensure sustained protection against rabies. The findings highlight the importance of locally grounded evaluations in urban settings, where growing populations and dense dog ownership create unique epidemiological challenges.

news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Isaias World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Atlanta | News Weather Meet Our Team News Tips 65° Contact Us Download with Damez Download Our App Advertise Memorials Watch CBS News Local News Dead bat found in Loganville backyard tests positive for rabies, officials say By Dan Raby Dan Raby Senior Digital Producer, CBS News Atlanta Dan Raby, the senior digital producer for CBS News Atlanta, has been covering everything happening around Georgia for more than a decade. Read Full Bio Dan Raby October 9, 2026 / 12:05 PM EDT / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google Health authorities in Gwinnett County are urging residents to use caution after a bat found dead in a Loganville resident's backyard tested positive for rabies. Officials say the animal was found behind a home on the 700 block of Autumn Meadow Drive on Oct. 6. The positive rabies case came about a month after another dead bat tested positive for rabies in the county. In that case, the bat was found inside a Snellville home. Georgia is a rabies-endemic state, which means the virus can be found in wildlife year-round. Officials say that means it's important for residents to make sure their pets are up-to-date on their vaccinations and avoid animals that may be behaving in unusual ways. The National Association of State Health Veterinarians says all unvaccinated dogs and cats exposed to a rabid animal need to be quarantined for four months and vaccinated one month before being released. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says rabies attacks the central nervous system and is nearly always fatal once symptoms develop. Early symptoms in people can include fever, headache, weakness and general discomfort. If you have been bitten or scratched by any stray animals or an animal suspected to have rabies, seek medical care immediately and let your provider know about the possible exposure. After that, contact GNR Public Health at (770) 339-4260 and ask for the on-call epidemiologist. To report any animal behaving in an unusual way, call the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement Bite Office at 770-339-3200, ext. 5576. news.content_zh: 据卫生当局称,在佐治亚州格温内特县洛根维尔居民后院发现的一只死蝙蝠的 狂犬病 检测结果呈阳性。该病例于 2026 年 10 月 9 日报告,发生在该县发现另一只 狂犬病 阳性蝙蝠大约一个月后。这只蝙蝠是在 Autumn Meadow Drive 700 街区的一户人家后面发现的。官员建议居民采取预防措施,确保他们的宠物及时更新 疫苗接种,并避免动物表现出异常行为。他们还建议,如果被疑似患有 狂犬病 的流浪动物咬伤或抓伤,请立即就医。虽然没有与此事件相关的人类病例或死亡报告,但野生动物中 狂犬病 的存在凸显了警惕和预防措施的重要性。全国州卫生兽医协会指出,接触狂犬病动物的未接种疫苗的宠物应隔离四个月,并在释放前接种疫苗。我们鼓励居民联系 Gwinnett 动物福利和咬伤执法办公室,电话:770-339-3200,分机号 11。以获得进一步指导。

Why is rabies prevention emphasized in Missoula currently? topics: Rabies Missoula Bats Animal Services Pet vaccination Public health Infectious disease Rabies exposure MISSOULA, Mont. — Missoula Animal Services is advising pet owners to vaccine their animals after two bats recently tested positive for rabies in the Missoula area. Although bats are the most common rabies carriers in the county, officials say unvaccinated cats, dogs, and stay animals can also carry and spread the disease. If you encounter a bat, do not touch or handle the bat. People bitten by a bat should seek medical care immediately and report all exposures to the Missoula Public Health Infectious Disease Department at 406-258-3896. Residents can also report pet exposures to Missoula Animal Services at 406-541-7387. Learn more about rabies by clicking here. Missoula Animal Services released the following information: Powered By 10 Sterling CRE applies for tax increment financing to begin proposed development of Midtown Share Next Stay Following two recent positive rabies tests for bats in the Missoula area, Missoula Animal Services is reminding residents how to handle bat exposures and to vaccinate their cats and dogs against rabies. Rabies is a serious but preventable disease that affects the brain and nervous system. It’s almost always fatal once symptoms appear but can be prevented with quick medical treatment after exposure and by ensuring pets are vaccinated. Area bats are the most common rabies carriers in Missoula County, but unvaccinated pets like cats and dogs, as well as stray animals, can also carry the virus. Owners whose pets are not vaccinated or whose vaccinations have expired should contact their veterinarian to get them vaccinated as soon as possible. Residents who encounter a bat should take the following precautions: Never intentionally touch or try to handle a bat, whether it’s alive or dead. If you unintentionally come into contact with a bat, treat it like a possible rabies exposure and seek medical care as soon as possible. Bat bites can be small and undetectable, and treatment may be necessary even if there is no obvious bite. This guidance also applies if a bat is found in a room with a child or someone who was asleep, unattended or is cognitively impaired. If you discover a bat in a residence, or a bat acting unusual in a public area, call Animal Services at 406-541-7387. Report all possible human exposures to the Missoula Public Health Infectious Disease Department by calling 406-258-3896. All possible pet exposures should be reported to Missoula Animal Services by calling 406-541-7387. “While human rabies exposure is still incredibly rare, with these recent test results, we want to make sure people know what they should and shouldn’t do if they encounter a bat, indoors or outside,” said Animal Services Manager Holli Hargrove. “Animal Services is here to help, and we want folks to feel prepared and educated if they find themselves in this situation.” BE THE FIRST TO COMMENT More information on rabies is available online at https://missoulapublichealth.org/communities/current-health-issues/rabies/. Summary Penang has not reported any human rabies cases since 1975, nor any animal cases to date, as stated by State Youth, Sports, and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen. The Penang State Health Department and the Department of Veterinary Services continue to monitor the situation and remain prepared to respond to potential incidents. Public adherence to Ministry of Health guidelines for animal bites, such as seeking prompt medical attention, is advised. Meanwhile, a recent human rabies case in Kedah marked the state's first since 1998. Make Malay Mail your preferred source on Google Giving you news that matter to Malaysians. First Published: Monday, 05 Oct 2026 5:17 PM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter Subscribe GEORGE TOWN, Oct 5 — Penang has recorded no human rabies cases since the last two cases were reported in 1975, with the Penang State Health Department remaining on standby to respond to any possible cases. State Youth, Sports and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen said no animal rabies cases had also been detected in the state to date. “No new cases have been reported thus far, but we are always prepared to deal with any incidents,” he said at a press conference for the Penang state-level Clean, Smoke-Free Premises Programme at Food Bayana Medan here today. Gooi said the state government was also working with the Department of Veterinary Services to monitor the rabies situation in Penang. He advised the public to follow Ministry of Health guidelines if bitten by an animal, including seeking immediate medical attention at any healthcare facility to ensure those exposed to infection risks receive proper examination and appropriate treatment. On Sept 27, a 31-year-old man from Kubang Pasu, Kedah, died of rabies after reportedly being bitten by a stray dog in August, marking the first human rabies case reported in the state since 1998. — Bernama You May Also Like Related Articles Malaysia / 6 m ago Malaysia has spent decades digitising public healthcare.
