supplementary_news.content_title: How air-dropping rabies vaccines keeps the virus from spreading into Knoxville
supplementary_news.content: The Tennessee Department of Health and the U.S. Department of Agriculture are launching a multi-state initiative to distribute 2.4 million oral rabies vaccine baits to control the spread of the virus among raccoons. KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WATE) — The Tennessee Department of Health has joined forces with the U.S. Department of Agriculture to combat the spread of rabies by dropping oral rabies vaccine (ORV) baits over five states. The bait distribution program is part of an effort to prevent the spread of the rabies virus by wild animals, most often raccoons, to the west. The ORV bait is coated with fish oil and fishmeal crumbles, which give off a pungent odor and attract raccoons to them. When an animal bites into the bait, the vaccine coats the back of their throat and vaccinates them." RABORAL V-RG® coated sachet oral rabies vaccine baits distributed in Tennessee (Photo via USDA) "We're targeting raccoons because they seem to be an animal that people like to associate with or befriend, shall we say," said Betsy Haley, GIS planner and wildlife biologist for the National Rabies Management Program in USDA. "When [people] feed their animals outside, the raccoons come up, and they think it's cute. Well, by vaccinating the raccoons, we're helping to protect those pets, as well as those pet owners from potential rabies exposure." The USDA said a total of 2.4 million baits will be distributed in east Tennessee, western North Carolina, southwest Virginia, north central Alabama, and north Georgia. In Tennessee, over 200,000 baits will be dropped. Starting October 7 to 12, helicopters will drop baits in urban and suburban communities in Athens, Charleston, Collegedale, Decatur, Elizabethton, Erwin, Johnson City, Mountain City, and Riceville. Then, between October 15-25, low-flying airplanes will drop baits in rural areas in Bradley, Carter, Greene, Hamilton, Johnson, McMinn, Meigs, Polk, Rhea, Sullivan, Unicoi, and Washington counties. Don’t approach elk: NPS warning follows injury in Great Smoky Mountains The ORV baits have been distributed in Tennessee since 2002 as part of a larger effort to prevent the westward spread of raccoon rabies by creating a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains from the Canadian border to Alabama. Haley said the program has been very successful in preventing the spread west, with no cases making it through the zone to Knoxville. "We've pushed the raccoon rabies cases back to the very eastern tip there in the north-northeast part of the state as well as some southern areas around Chattanooga and Cleveland area we're still baiting, but for the most part in Tennessee it's working very well," said Haley. Rabies infects the central nervous system, causing inflammation of the brain and eventually death. While the disease is rare in humans, with only 1 to 3 cases reported a year according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it can have serious consequences. The majority of cases are found in wild animals, according to the CDC. "The hopes for these programs are to vaccinate as many raccoons as we can. These vaccine baits will work with other wildlife, but we are specifically targeting raccoons to try to reduce and potentially eliminate raccoon rabies variant from the environment," said Haley. Haley added that raccoons are the most common carrier of rabies in wildlife in the East. Because of this, the USDA asks people not to feed their animals outside and to keep their trash secured to limit contact with raccoons that could be carrying the virus. Could Tennessee try to execute Christa Pike again? Lawyer explains fallout, proposed legal changes The oral rabies vaccine bait packets will also be marked with a toll-free number (1-877-722-6725) for assistance or information if someone finds or comes in contact with a bait packet. "If you find the bait, don't freak out; don't automatically pick it up. If you need to move it, if it's in a spot where, say, it might have accidentally fallen on the sidewalk, or it's right on the edge of your yard, you can either use a paper towel or rubber gloves, pick it up and move it. And we say to do that just because the fish on the outside of the packet really does leave a pungent odor on your fingers," said Haley. Haley added that if a person or their pet comes into contact with the bait, it is not going to harm them. "It may, at worst, get an upset stomach from eating the bait, but don't try to take the bait out of the dog's mouth, because you could potentially expose yourself to the vaccine. And all that would do is potentially give you a rash. So, if you need to take it out of the dog's mouth, wash your hands really well with soap and water and keep an eye on that spot if you do get scratched," said Haley.
